questions.question: What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chronic tophaceous gout has the features of asymmetrical joint swellings, tophi and progressive cartilage and bone destruction. This condition can occur after several years of persistent gout. Typically present are tophi - solid deposits of monosodium urate crystals in the joints, cartilage, bones and elsewhere in the body. The tophi can occasionally break through the skin and appear as yellowish/white chalky nodules that have been described as looking like crab eyes. Gout is often associated with a high alcohol intake along with certain pharmacological agents such as thiazide diuretics and the immunosuppressant cyclosporine often used to prevent rejection in kidney transplant patients.

questions.question: A 25-year-old lady with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis has severe Raynaud's phenomenon, skin tightness, sclerodactyly and skin thickening to the shoulders. She presents to the EAU with a three month history of gradually worsening shortness of breath. There is no history of orthopnoea. Her exercise tolerance has diminished from 500 yards to less than 50 yards. On examination, the JVP is raised, and there is mild bi-pedal oedema. The BP is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 109/min, SaO is 91% on air, respiratory rate is 20/min. Muscle strength is normal. Examination of heart, lungs and abdomen is unremarkable. Investigations show: Hb 121 g/L (115-165) WBC 7.8 ×10 /L (4-11) Neutrophils 70% (40-75) Platelet 270 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 36 mm/hr (0-20) U&E's and creatinine normal D-dimers negative CXR normal ECG right axis deviation What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This patient developed pulmonary artery hypertension as a complication of systemic sclerosis. Systemic sclerosis is a chronic autoimmune disease characterised by increased fibroblast activity and fibrosis in a number of different organ systems. 90-95% of patients have positive antinuclear antibodies. There are two major subtypes: Limited cutaneous and Diffuse cutaneous. CREST syndrome is an older term for the limited cutaneous form (calcinosis, Raynauds' phenomenon, oeosophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia). Patients with systemic sclerosis can present with skin abnormalities, musculoskeletal changes, gastrointestinal complications, pulmonary disease, renal crisis and dry eyes and mouth. Pulmonary hypertension can present in isolation in systemic sclerosis, or in association with interstitial lung disease or cardiac dysfunction. It is a frequent cause of morbidity and mortality. In pulmonary hypertension, the electrocardiogram may demonstrate signs of right ventricular hypertrophy, such as tall right precordial R waves, right axis deviation, right bundle branch block and right ventricular strain (increased P-wave amplitude in lead II). The higher the pulmonary artery pressure, the more sensitive the ECG. The chest radiograph is inferior to the ECG in detecting pulmonary hypertension, but it may show prominent pulmonary arteries or evidence of underlying lung disease. Despite advances in echocardiography and biomarkers, right heart catheterisation remains the diagnostic test to differentiate pulmonary veno-occlusive disease from hypertension. This is essential because pulmonary vasodilator therapy can increase mortality in veno-occlusive disease. Recent studies have investigated the use of non-invasive screening, but their use remains controversial. Treatment options are limited, and prognosis is worse than with idiopathic pulmonary hypertension. Median survival is one year from diagnosis. Extrapulmonary disease in systemic sclerosis limit candidacy for lung transplantation. New therapies that target abnormal cellular proliferation in the pulmonary vasculature are currently under investigation. An ECG without ST segment or T wave changes does not support the diagnosis of unstable angina, and there is no history of chest pain. Congestive cardiac failure is unlikely in a 25-year-old, and there is no history of orthopnoea which would be typical. Pulmonary venous hypertension occurs in response to left heart failure. There are no signs or symptoms of left heart failure in this patient. Fibrosing alveolitis is unlikely in the absence of crepitations, and in the presence of a normal CXR. Reference: 1. Chatterjee S. Pulmonary hypertension in systemic sclerosis. Semin Arthritis Rheum. 2011;41:19-37. 2. Mathai SC, Hassoun PM. Pulmonary arterial hypertension associated with systemic sclerosis. Expert Rev Respir Med. 2011;5:267-279 3. Nauser TD, Stites SW. Diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary hypertension. Am Fam Physician. 2001;63:1789-98. 4. York M, Farber HW. Pulmonary hypertension: screening and evaluation in scleroderma. Curr Opin Rheumatol. 2011;23:536-44.

questions.question: An 82-year-old gentleman is referred to your outpatient clinic by his GP. He gives a two month history of proximal muscle stiffness, especially in the morning. He denies any weakness. What is the next best investigation?
questions.explanation: The brief history is suggestive of polymyalgia rheumatica: proximal muscle stiffness but not weakness in an elderly patient. Weakness and muscle pain are the predominant features of polymyositis. While each of the other tests listed might be relevant in the broad work-up of this patient, a high ESR would prompt immediate treatment with steroids. Polymyalgia is often associated with giant cell arteritis - prompt treatment may prevent blindness.

questions.question: A 37-year-old woman who recently started gardening presents with pain on the lateral aspect of her right wrist. This is worsened by making a fist, and by using heavy gardening tools. On examination, there is tenderness, and swelling around the lateral margin of the right wrist, extending a few centimeters proximally. Finkelstein's test is positive. Recent FBC, UEC, LFTs and rheumatoid factor have been negative. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: DeQuervain's tenosynovitis occurs in the first extensor compartment on the back of the thumb. It involves abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons. There is localised pain, worsened by aggravating motion and swelling. Localised tenderness may be present. Finkelstein's test - exacerbation of symptoms on flexion of thumb, and ulnar deviation of wrist - may be present but is not pathognomonic of DeQuervain's tenosynovitis. Intersection syndrome is tenosynovitis of the extensor carpi radialis tendons, where these tendons are crossed by abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons. The pain and swelling is present 4 cm proximal to the wrist joint. Preiser's disease and Kienbock's disease are avascular necrosis of scaphoid and lunate bones respectively, and present with pain and swelling in the wrist joint. Dupuytren's contracture is a condition of nodular hypertrophy and contractures of the superficial palmar fascia. Patients present with pitting, and nodule and thickening of the fascia of the hand.

questions.question: A 69-year-old lady presents to you complaining of being non-specifically unwell over the last month. She is stiff especially in the mornings and has difficulty lifting her hands to comb her hair. Her arms and shoulders ache constantly and she has jaw pain when chewing. She has lost 4 kg in weight and has a persistent headache. She smokes 10 cigarettes a day and consumes 10 units of alcohol a week. On examination, temperature is 38°C, pulse 84 beats/min and BP 125/80 mmHg. The examination is otherwise unremarkable. Investigations show: Hb 99 g/L (115-165) WCC 13.9 ×10 /L (4-11) Platelets 400 ×10 /L (150-400) Plasma sodium 139 mmol/L (137-144) Plasma potassium 4.7 mmol/L (3.5-4.9) Plasma urea 5.0 mmol/L (2.5-7.5) Plasma creatinine 109 µmol/L (60-110) Plasma glucose 5.9 mmol/L (3.0-6.0) Bilirubin 15 µmol/L (1-22) Plasma alkaline phosphatase 390 U/L (45-105) Plasma aspartate transaminase 65 U/L (1-31) Plasma creatine kinase 150 U/L (24-170) What is the most appropriate investigation to be performed next?
questions.explanation: Polymyalgia rheumatica/temporal arteritis may be associated with: Predominantly polymyalgia symptoms, for example, proximal muscle pain, stiffness, or Arteritis symptoms, for example, headaches, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication. Systemic involvement is common, for example, fever, malaise and weight loss. Typically the ESR is very high. The main reason to diagnose and treat the condition is to prevent blindness.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman presents with pain at the base of her right thumb. There is tenderness and swelling of the right first carpometacarpal joint. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: E. Avascular necrosis of the scaphoid
questions.explanation: The first carpometacarpal joint is a frequent site of osteoarthritis in postmenopausal women. Clinical features include tenderness, stiffness, crepitus, swelling and pain on abduction of the thumb. Squaring of the hand, caused by swelling, radial subluxation of the metacarpal and atrophy of the thenar muscles, is a characteristic clinical sign. Scaphoid fractures are relatively common, typically occurring following a fall onto outstretched hand. The proximal portion lacks its own blood supply, so avascular necrosis can occur if a fracture leaves it isolated from the remainder of the scaphoid. This produces pain and tenderness of the radial side of the wrist, classically in the anatomical snuffbox rather than the base of the thumb, exacerbated by wrist movement. De Quervain's tenosynovitis disease is a common pathology which consists of a stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal compartment of the wrist. It typically presents with pain on the radial aspect of the wrist, with associated swelling and tenderness. Treatment is with splinting, with or without corticosteroid injection. Reference: 1. Ilyas AM, at al. De quervain tenosynovitis of the wrist. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2007;15:757-64. 2. Peter JB, Marmor L. Osteoarthritis of the first carpometacarpal joint. Calif Med. 1968;109:116-20.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman was referred to clinic for an opinion regarding a three month history of fatigue, generalised weakness, easy bruising and joint pains. On examination she appeared pale. The spleen was palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin. The remainder of the examination was normal. Investigations showed: Haemoglobin 95 g/L (115-165) MCV 95 fL (80-96) White cell count 2.1 ×10 /L (4-11) Platelets 55 ×10 /L (150-400) What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of pancytopenia, arthralgia and splenomegaly makes SLE the most likely diagnosis. Acute leukaemias are associated with elevated white cell counts often accompanied by leukaemia and thrombocytopenia; hepatosplenomegaly is usually a feature of ALL rather than AML. ITP may be associated with thrombocytopenia and splenomegaly, but is not associated with penias of myeloid and lymphoid cell lines. Patients with longstanding rheumatoid arthritis may develop Felty's syndrome (leucopenia and splenomegaly; often accompanied by anaemia and thrombocytopenia) but this follows years of active rheumatoid disease. Myelodysplastic syndromes present with anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia but is associated with macrocytosis; MDS is a disease of older people.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man has had a painful, swollen right knee and difficulty walking over the last three days. He has had two self-limiting episodes of severe pain and swelling in the right big toe in the last year. A knee aspirate shows leucocytes but no organisms on Gram stain, and negatively birefringent crystals on polarised light microscopy. Recent blood tests show normal renal function, and a raised serum urate 452 µmol/L (210-415 µmol/L). What is the next step in his long term management, once the current episode of acute synovitis has settled?
questions.explanation: The British Society of Rheumatology guidelines state that the plasma urate should be maintained below 300 µmol/L in the management of gout. Drug therapy (allopurinol in the first instance) is indicated to achieve this if: A second attack occurs within one year of the initial presentation Tophi are present The patient has renal insufficiency There are also uric acid stones, and Diuretics cannot be stopped. However, it is important to remember that commencement of uric acid lowering drug therapy should be delayed until one to two weeks after the initial episode has resolved. Colchicine should be co-prescribed for the first six months. Febuxostat is a non-purine selective inhibitor of xanthine oxidase. that reduces serum uric acid concentration. NICE guidance recommends its use only in patients who are intolerant of allopurinol or for whom allopurinol is contraindicated. Oral, intramuscular or intra-articular corticosteroids are effective in the control of acute gout, however prolonged use is associated with significant side effects and they are therefore not indicated in the long term management. Similarly, ibuprofen may be used to treat acute gout, but has no role in the long term management of gout. Lifestyle advice is also critical in the management of gout, but is unlikely to work in isolation in this case where there have been recurrent acute episodes. You should recommend patients restrict the amount of red meat, foods rich in purines (liver, kidneys, seafood) and alcohol. In addition dehydration should be avoided, and patients should be encouraged to take regular exercise and stop smoking. Although not needed to answer this question, it is important you also understand how to manage an acute episode of gout. The principles are: Commence anti-inflammatory medication immediately, and continue for two weeks. NSAIDs are first line in conjunction with gastro-protective medication where indicated. Colchicine is an alternative but is slower to work and can be associated with significant diarrhoea. Rest the affected joints Allopurinol should not be started during an acute attack but in patients already established on allopurinol it should be continued If diuretics are being used to treat hypertension an alternative antihypertensive should be considered, but they should not be stopped in the presence of heart failure Corticosteroids are highly effective, and can be used where NSAIDs are not tolerated, or in refractory disease (intra-articular, oral, intramuscular, intravenous). Reference: Jordan KM, et al. British Society for Rheumatology and British Health Professionals in Rheumatology guideline for the management of gout. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2007;46:1372-4.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man presented with a six week history of general malaise and a two day history of a right foot drop, a left ulnar nerve palsy and a widespread purpuric rash. He complained of arthralgia but had no clinical evidence of inflammatory joint disease. Investigations revealed: ESR 100 mm/hr (0-20) ANCA Negative ANA Negative Rheumatoid factor Strongly positive C3 0.8 g/L (0.75-1.6) C4 0.02 g/L (0.14-0.5) Urine dipstick Blood ++, No protein An echocardiogram was normal and two sets of blood cultures were negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The history is strongly suggestive of systemic vasculitis with mononeuritis multiplex, purpuric rash and haematuria. It is important to exclude conditions which can mimic vasculitis such as infective endocarditis. The normal echocardiogram and negative blood cultures make this unlikely. Whilst polyarteritis nodosa can present with exactly this clinical picture, the marked consumption of C4 together with a strongly positive rheumatoid factor strongly suggests cryoglobulinaemia as the underlying cause. Cryoglobulins are immunoglobulins which precipitate in the cold. They can be Type I (monoclonal) Type II (mixed monoclonal and polyclonal) or Type III (polyclonal). Type I cryoglobulinaemia is associated with haematological diseases such as myeloma and Waldenstrom's. Type II and Type III cryoglobulinaemia can be associated with many connective tissue disorders, chronic infections and most importantly, hepatitis C infection which should always be excluded. Treatment of cryoglobulinaemia would include plasmaphoresis, high dose steroids and cyclophosphamide. The following conditions may be associated with a positive rheumatoid factor: Rheumatoid arthritis - 26 to 90% Sjögren's syndrome - 75 to 95% Mixed connective tissue disease - 50 to 60% Mixed cryoglobulinemia (types II and III) - 40 to 100% Systemic lupus erythematosus - 15 to 35% Polymyositis/dermatomyositis - 5 to 10%

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman with knee OA, past history of peptic ulcers, and ischaemic heart disease presents with a one year history of worsening bilateral, anterior knee pain. The pain is increased by walking and climbing stairs. There is no history of knee swelling. The pain is partially controlled by co-codamol (30/500 mg), two tablets up to four times a day, NSAID gel, and capsaicin cream. On examination, she is overweight. There is crepitus and during active and passive movement of both knees. There is no knee effusion. What is the next step in her management?
questions.explanation: This patient has knee pain resistant to several simple analgesics. The next step in her treatment is to start her on stronger opiates. There is not enough evidence that acupuncture or chondroitin sulphate is clinically or cost effective in osteoarthritis (OA). Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may be used for short term pain relief of severe symptomatic knee OA, however, the use of NSAIDs for long term pain control in OA is discouraged. Long term oral NSAIDs are potentially dangerous as they may lead to renal failure, fluid retention, peptic ulcers, and are contraindicated in this patient as she has a history of peptic ulcers. Cox-2 inhibitors have a much lower risk of gastrointestinal bleed. However, as they increase the risk of cardiovascular events, they should not be prescribed to those with cardiovascular disease, or in those with high risk of cardiovascular disease.

questions.question: A 25-year-old Caucasian farmer presents to the outpatient department complaining of a two month history of generalised aches and pains. He used to be an active runner but says a hip injury forced him to give up competitive running a year ago. Two years ago he was seen in the Emergency department with a painful red eye for which he was treated with eye drops. He is a heavy smoker of 45 cigarettes a day and consumes five pints of beer every weekend. He denies any skin rashes or mucosal ulceration. His mother suffered from rheumatoid arthritis and his father had severe gout. On examination, the left first metatarsophalangeal joint was swollen and tense, but all the other joints were unremarkable. Rotation of the lumbar spine was restricted. Which of the following tests would be most useful in establishing the diagnosis?
options: C. Serial serum uric acid levels
E. Examination of joint fluid for crystals
questions.explanation: A history of joint pains, in particular that of the lumbar spine, ocular involvement (uveitis) and the absence of mucosal ulceration in a male would suggest a differential diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis and reactive arthritis. The earliest radiographic change in ankylosing spondylitis is usually sacroiliitis, which may also be seen in reactive arthritis. HLA-B27 antigen typing is present in 90% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis and 75% with reactive arthritis. However, it is present in only 8% of the normal Caucasian population.

questions.question: A 54-year-old patient with tophaceous gout developed hypersensitivity reaction to allopurinol tablets. He is offered long-term urate-lowering treatment with febuxostat. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of febuxostat?
questions.explanation: Febuxostat is a non-purine, selective inhibitor of xanthine oxidase; unlike allopurinol, which is a purine analogue inhibitor of xanthine oxidase. Uricosuric agents, like probenecid and benzbromarone, work by blocking the anion exchanger URAT-1 at the apical brush border membrane of the proximal tubule in kidneys. They also block urate reabsorption at the basolateral membrane of these cells by blocking GLUT 9 - the electrogenic glucose and fructose transport facilitator.

questions.question: A 64-year-old patient with sero-positive erosive RA has active inflammatory arthritis despite treatment with methotrexate (20 mg/week), and sulfasalazine (1 gram bd). He is offered treatment with biological agents. Of the various options available, he chooses to stat abatacept. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of abatacept?
questions.explanation: Abatacept is a cytotoxic lymphocyte antigen 4 (CTLA 4) homologue - licensed for RA treatment. Adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, golimumab, and certolizumab are anti-TNF alpha agents. Rituximab is an anti-CD 20 antibody - licensed for RA treatment. Anakinra is an anti-IL 1 antibody.

questions.question: You are referred a 42-year-old nurse who works in a liver transplant unit. She complains of two months of intermittent episodes of joint pains with occasional swelling of the wrists and knees. These episodes last one to three days and are helped by ibuprofen. However, her knee pain is increasingly worse and her fingers are more stiff and sore. About a month ago, she started to notice a rash on her legs which appeared worse when she was up during the day. The rash was not painful and looked like 'blood blisters'. The rash spontaneously subsided after about 10 days, but has reappeared in the last week or so. In addition, she has began to develop painful purple lesions on her ankles. Over the last two weeks, she has begun to experience low grade fevers, muscle aches and recurrent headaches. She assumed these were flu symptoms and has therefore missed several days of work. Her appetite has not been good and she has noticed some weight loss. Two days ago, she began to develop abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. On examination, she looks ill. Pulse 120 beats/min, BP 140/90 mmHg, temperature 39°C. Mucosae are dry with no lesions. Heart sounds are normal with no murmurs. Chest examination is unremarkable. She has mild right upper quadrant tenderness but no guarding. No hepatosplenomegaly is noted and rectal examination is normal. Neurological examination is unremarkable. She has mild swelling and tenderness of both wrists and small bilateral knee effusions. On her legs, discrete palpable purpuric lesions are noted with a few tender haemorrhagic lesions over both ankles. Investigations show: Hb 108 g/L (115-165) WCC 12.2 ×10 /L (4-11) Platelets 350 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 60 mm/hr (0-20) Plasma sodium 144 mmol/L (137-144) Plasma potassium 3.8 mmol/L (3.5-4.9) Plasma urea 7.1 mmol/L (2.5-7.5) Plasma creatinine 110 µmol/L (60-110) Plasma bilirubin 55 µmol/L (1-22) Plasma aspartate transaminase 107 U/L (1-31) Plasma alkaline phosphatase 119 U/L (45-105) Plasma albumin 40 g/L (37-49) Anti-nuclear antibody Negative Rheumatoid titre 1:160 Chest x ray Mild cardiomegaly Blood cultures No growth after 24 hours Urinalysis +++ blood +++ protein 10-20 red blood cells/high power field 5-10 white blood cells/high power field Granular casts detected What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
options: E. Polyarteritis nodosa with microscopic polyarteritis overlap
questions.explanation: A positive anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) result is present in nearly all cases of systemic lupus erythematosus, thus a negative ANA means anti-double stranded antibody is not indicated. Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) should always be done in suspected systemic vasculitis. In polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) and vasculitis associated with microscopic polyarteritis, anti-cytoplasmic antibodies directed against myeloperoxidase (pANCA) will produce a perinuclear staining pattern and is seen in up to 60% with the overlap syndrome (compared to <10%with PAN alone). In granulomatosis with polyangiitis , a cytoplasmic pattern is likely, indicating antibodies to proteinase-3. A positive hepatitis B surface antigen is associated with polyarteritis nodosa of medium and small arteries. Polyclonal gammaglobulinaemia on serum protein electrophoresis would be expected in systemic inflammatory disease and does not aid diagnosis. The rest of the tests listed would give non-specific changes and not be helpful in establishing a diagnosis. The patient has necrotising vasculitis of the skin, kidneys, gut and joints. In addition, she has systemic features of fever, malaise and weight loss. The best diagnosis is polyarteritis nodosa associated with hepatitis B. The negative serology makes systemic lupus erythematosus less likely. The negative serial blood cultures makes endocarditis-related arthropathy less likely. Henoch-Schönlein purpura is more common in children. Although, rheumatoid factor is positive, there is no clear involvement of the proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints which is common in rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman presents with deteriorating wheeze and dyspnoea. She has been diagnosed with asthma over the last 15 years and is treated with inhaled salbutamol, inhaled fluticasone and has received numerous courses of prednisolone. Currently, she is receiving 15 mg of prednisolone daily as a reducing dose. Four years ago, she had also received cyclical hormone replacement therapy (HRT) for post-menopausal flushes but this was stopped after one year of therapy when she developed a deep vein thrombosis. What treatment would you select as prophylaxis against osteoporosis?
questions.explanation: This patient is at high risk of developing osteoporosis being post-menopausal and receiving high doses of steroids. Of the therapies listed the most appropriate is the bisphosphonate, alendronate. NICE guidelines suggest the use of bisphosphonates where steroids are used over the longer term for the prevention of osteoporosis. This treatment should be for 3-5 years and patients should be made aware that it is not preventative but reduces risk. Calcitonin is administered subcutaneously and is not appropriate. Raloxifene is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) and is an appropriate therapy for the prevention and treatment of post-menopausal osteoporosis but like HRT may be associated with an increased risk of thromboembolism and should not be used in this case. Calcium and vitamin D are useful adjuncts but would not prevent steroid induced osteoporosis. Reference: NICE. Osteoporosis: assessing the risk of fragility fracture (CG146).

questions.question: A 47-year-old woman with longstanding diabetes presents with a painful, stiff left shoulder of three weeks duration. The pain is dull, aching and present at rest. Shoulder movements are reduced. There is no history of trauma, temperature, or night pain. On examination, the shoulder movements are globally restricted. There is no evidence of shoulder effusion. Cervical spine movements are normal. Recent FBC, UEC, LFT, and bone profile are normal. What is the most likely cause of her shoulder symptoms?
questions.explanation: This patient has adhesive capsulitis. Adhesive capsulitis (synonym, frozen shoulder) is common in diabetics. In this condition there is a fairly acute onset of dull pain, and global restriction of shoulder movements. Pain is frequently present at rest. External rotation is the most severely affected movement. Subacromial bursitis presents with shoulder pain when trying to reach above the head. During examination, pain is present in the mid arc of shoulder abduction. There is usually no rest pain. Active shoulder abduction is limited by pain. However, there is full range of shoulder abduction passively. Rotator cuff tears present with symptoms similar to subacromial impingement. There may be weakness in specific shoulder movements in full thickness rotator cuff tears. Osteoarthritis at glenohumeral and acromioclavicular joints usually presents with gradually worsening, generalised shoulder, or shoulder tip pain, in older people, or in those with physically demanding jobs.

questions.question: A 22-year-old man with known hereditary angioneurotic oedema (HAO) presents with a recurrent fever, arthralgia and a rash on the face and the upper chest. Despite treatment for his HAO, he has always been troubled by recurrent attacks and has required adrenaline on several occasions. His C4 levels have been persistently reduced secondary to his HAO. What is the most likely cause for his current symptoms?
questions.explanation: HAO is characterised by deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor. This leads to persistent activation of the classical complement pathway and C4 levels are frequently low secondary to activation and consumption. If treatment fails to normalise the C4 levels and they remain persistently low; these patients are at an increased risk of developing SLE.

questions.question: A 44-year-old man has a one month history of painful, and swollen right hand index, and middle finger distal interphalangeal joint. He recounts a few episodes when one of the fingers in his left hand swelled up. However, they subsided completely after a week. He drinks 6 units of alcohol/week and has just returned from USA. There is no significant past or family history except that his sister has psoriasis. On examination there are swollen and tender distal interphalangeal joints in right hand index and middle finger. The results of a recent blood test are as follows: Haemoglobin 130 g/L (130-180) WBC 10.9 ×10 /L (4-11) Neutrophils 6.8 ×10 /L (1.5-7) ESR 45 mm/hr (0-15) Urea, electrolytes and creatinine are normal Rheumatoid factor - negative What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This patient has psoriatic arthritis. In the absence of psoriasis, a positive family history of psoriasis in a first degree relative supports the diagnosis of psoriatic arthritis. There are five different patterns of joint involvement which can occur in psoriatic arthritis. One is predominant distal interphalyngeal joint involvement associated with nail pitting, and onycholysis (separation of nail from nail bed) in that finger. The second is a rheumatoid arthritis type pattern, with proximal interphalyngeal joint involvement. The third is large joint oligoarthritis, and the fourth is a predominantly axial pattern. The final, and thankfully rare, form is arthritis mutilans where destruction of the metacarpals results in telescoping of the fingers. The absence of preceding infection makes reactive arthritis unlikely. Rheumatoid arthritis is unlikely as there is asymmetrical joint involvement - with predominant involvement of the distal interphalangeal joints in the hands. DIP joint involvement is rare in RA. Gout is unlikely. The alcohol intake is not excessive, and except for male gender, there is no other significant risk factor, for example, age more than 40, diuretic use, renal failure and solid organ transplant. Palindromic rheumatism is said to be present when there are episodes of joint swelling, which last for a few days, and migrate across the patient's body.

questions.question: A 55-year-old lady with RA (RF positive, anti-CCP positive) presented with multiple well defined ulcers on her legs. She was on methotrexate 20 mg/week, folic acid 5 mg/day and sulfasalazine 1 gm/day. Her arthritis is well controlled, with no swollen or tender joints. Her blood tests showed leucopenia - see below, and the methotrexate, sulfasalazine were stopped for two weeks. Repeat blood tests did not show any improvement in WBC count. Investigations show: Hb 129 g/L (115-165) WBC 1.4 ×10 /L (4-11) Neutrophils 39% (40-75) Platelet 166 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 26 mm/hr (0-30) CRP 13 mg/L (<10) Urea, electrolytes and creatinine are normal. Anti-nuclear antibody: negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) frequently develop neutropenia. Common causes are: Drug related - in which case it would improve with time, or Due to Felty's syndrome - a triad of splenomegaly and pancytopenia (predominantly neutropenia) in someone with longstanding seropositive RA. Rheumatoid vasculitis is rare, and presents with a vasculitic rash, neuropathy, and high inflammatory markers. Co-existence of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and RA may occur (rhupus), however this patient is ANA negative, which makes SLE very unlikely.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man with Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, previously treated with cyclophosphamide, and pulse methylprednisolone is on cyclosporine (100 mg/day), and on a reducing course of oral prednisolone (15 mg/day to 7.5 mg/day) for the last two months. His vasculitis is well controlled. He was found to have worsening hypertension, despite starting on amlodipine and doxazosin. Urine dipstick and renal ultrasound are normal. He has normal inflammatory markers and FBC over the last few months. His blood tests are as follows: 0 week 2 weeks 6 weeks 8 weeks BP (mmHg) 140/90 145/95 150/100 160/110 Na (mmol/L) 142 140 141 139 K (mmol/L) 4.5 4.7 5.0 5.0 Urea (µmol/L) 10.2 12.4 12.6 14.2 Creat (µmol/L) 110 135 170 190 What is the most likely cause for deteriorating renal function?
questions.explanation: Serious side effects of cyclosporine include hypertension, and renal impairment. Difficult to control hypertension and an increase in creatinine by more than 30% from baseline are indications for stopping cyclosporine treatment. There is no evidence of active vasculitis in this patient; the inflammatory markers and urine dipstick are normal. Cushing's syndrome does not lead to renal impairment, and hypertension and renal impairment are not delayed adverse events of cyclophosphamide.

questions.question: A 69-year-old lady presents to you complaining of being non-specifically unwell over the last month. She is stiff especially in the mornings and has difficulty lifting her hands to comb her hair. Her arms and shoulders ache constantly and she has jaw pain when chewing. She has lost 4 kg in weight and has a persistent headache. She smokes 10 cigarettes a day and consumes 10 units of alcohol a week. Apart from tenderness with reduced mobility in the proximal muscles of her arms and legs, examination is normal. Investigations show: Hb 99 g/L (115-165) WCC 13.9 ×10 /L (4-11) Platelets 400 ×10 /L (150-400) Plasma sodium 139 mmol/L (137-144) Plasma potassium 4.7 mmol/L (3.5-4.9) Plasma urea 5.0 mmol/L (2.5-7.5) Plasma creatinine 109 µmol/L (60-110) Plasma glucose 5.9 mmol/L (3.0-6.0) Bilirubin 15 µmol/L (1-22) Plasma alkaline phosphatase 87 U/L (45-105) Plasma aspartate transaminase 29 U/L (1-31) ESR 92 mm/hr (<30) What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Polymyalgia rheumatica/temporal arteritis may be associated with: Predominantly polymyalgia symptoms, for example, proximal muscle pain and stiffness, or Arteritis symptoms, for example, headaches, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication and Systemic features, for example, fever, malaise and weight loss. Weakness is not typically a feature but may be apparent due to pain or stiffness with weight loss. Typically the ESR is very high. Temporal arteritis must be treated with high dose steroids if suspected as it can result in blindness. This fact is important as it reminds us that temporal arteritis, although commonly affecting the temporal artery, is a vasculitis affecting medium and large sized arteries throughout the body, hence its other term 'giant cell arteritis'. The superficial temporal artery supplies the orbit of the eye and is a branch of the external carotid artery; the ophthalmic artery supplies the majority of the blood to the eye itself and is a branch of the internal carotid artery. It is inflammation and therefore narrowing of this vessel that may cause blindness.

questions.question: A 25-year-old lady gives birth to a baby with complete heart block who subsequently requires pacemaker insertion. Which of the following antibodies is most likely to be detected in the maternal serum?
questions.explanation: The majority of cases of congenital heart block are due to the presence of anti-Ro/SSA antibodies in the maternal serum. The mother may have no evidence of a connective tissue disorder. The risks of congenital heart block in mothers with anti-Ro/SSA antibodies remains very small (less than 3%) but the correlation between the presence of anti-Ro/SSA antibodies and congenital heart block is very strong. The heart block is generally permanent (unlike other features of neonatal lupus) and insertion of a permanent pacemaker is frequently required.

questions.question: A 42-year-old female presented with acute back pain after lifting a chair. The pain is intense, increases on movement, and radiates bilaterally to the hypochondriacal region. Upon questioning she denied previous fractures, but admitted to a gradual loss of height (5 cm from her young adult height) and occasional self-limiting back pain. Past medical history included spontaneous menopause at the age of 37. She had never taken any regular medications, calcium or vitamin D supplements in the past. Examination revealed a thin woman who had a dorsal hyperkyphosis. Severe back pain was ellicited on movement and local percussion. Investigations showed: Bone mineral density (BMD) was assessed by dual-energy x ray absorptiometry at the hip and the lumbar spine (L1-L4). BMD T-score at lumbar spine −3.0 BMD T-score at total hip −2.8 What is the diagnosis?
options: B. Post menopausal osteoporotic vertebral fractures
C. Osteomalacia secondary to Vitamin D or calcium deficiency
D. Vertebral fractures secondary to malignant infiltration
questions.explanation: This lady has several risk factors for post-menopausal osteoporosis, including Early onset (<45 years) menopause Absence of hormone replacement therapy, calcium and vitamin D supplemention and Low body weight. Patients with osteoporosis may have no warning signs until the first fracture occurs. Gradual height loss and dorsal kyphosis may result from microfractures or complete fractures of vertebral bodies. A T-score refers to the difference in standard deviation (SD) from the mean bone mass. The World Health Organisation (WHO) criteria for the diagnosis of osteoporosis is as follows: T-score Normal, ≥−1.0 Osteopenia −1.0 to −2.5 Osteoporosis ≤−2.5 Causes of secondary osteoporosis such as bone metastasis and myeloma must be excluded when a vertebral fracture is found.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man has had a painful right knee and difficulty in walking for three years. He had diabetes, hypertension, CKD 3 (eGFR 45 ml/min). He is on aspirin, amlodipine, metformin, and citalopram. During routine tests, his serum urate was checked. This was 521 μmol/L (210-415). What is the next step in his management?
questions.explanation: Uric acid is the final product of purine metabolism. Raised levels are most commonly associated with gout, but more recently they have been identified as a marker for a number of metabolic and haemodynamic abnormalities (including ischaemic heart disease, diabetes mellitus, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia). Blood levels depend of the rate of breakdown and excretion, and most cases of hyperuricaemia are associated with defective elimination. Causes of hyperuricaemia include: Underexcretion: Renal impairment Metabolic syndrome Drugs, e.g. diuretics, low-dose aspirin, cyclosporin, tacrolimus, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, levodopa, nicotinic acid Acidosis Pre-eclampsia and eclampsia Hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism Sarcoidosis Familial juvenile gouty nephropathy Chronic lead intoxication Trisomy 21 Idiopathic. Overproduction: Purine rich diet Tumour lysis syndrome HGPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan and Kelley-Seegmiller syndromes) Increased PRPP synthetase activity Idiopathic. Combined: Alcohol Exercise Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency Aldolase B deficiency. Management of hyperuricaemia relies on determining whether the patient is symptomatic or asymptomatic, and identifying aetiology and comorbidities. Symptomatic patients present with gout and nephrolithiasis. Most patients with hyperuricaemia never develop gout or stones. Treatment of these patients is not considered beneficial or cost-effective, and is therefore generally not recommended. The exception to this is in patients at risk of tumour lysis syndrome, where prophylactic treatment is recommended to reduce the incidence of renal impairment. Allopurinol is the mainstay of treatment for hyperuricaemia. However, treatment depends on the cause and clinical setting and newer agents such as rasburicase and pegloticase are increasing in use.

questions.question: A 40-year-old insulin-dependent man with poorly controlled diabetes presents with an acutely erythematous and swollen right mid foot which he has experienced for the last three weeks. He drinks alcohol socially, and has had no recent injuries to the foot. On examination, the mid foot is warm. Pedal pulses are intact. There is sensory loss in a glove and stocking distribution bilaterally. Recent blood tests show a normal FBC, CRP, and UEC, and a foot radiograph is normal. What is the next step in his management?
options: D. Immobilise in a plaster cast
questions.explanation: In patients with long-standing diabetes and peripheral neuropathy, a red hot swollen foot should raise suspicion of Charcot neuroarthropathy. Charcot neuropathy presents as a warm, swollen, erythematous foot and ankle, and infection is important to exclude. The majority of patients are in their 50-60s, and they often present in the latter stages of the disease. It can occur in association with a variety of conditions, including leprosy, poliomyelitis, rheumatoid arthritis, although today the most common cause is diabetes mellitus. The pathophysiology of Charcot neuroarthropathy is not completely understood, but is thought to start with peripheral neuropathy. The lack of pain sensation may mean that patients subject the foot joints (commonly the mid foot) to stress injuries that lead to the Charcot process. It is important to note however that about half of patients present with pain. Four stages of Charcot neuropathy are recognised: Stage 0 (inflammation) - characterised by erythema and oedema, but no structural changes. Stage 1 (development) - bone resorption, fragmentation and joint dislocation. Swelling, warmth and erythema persist but there are also radiographic changes such as debris formation at the articular margins, osseous fragmentation and joint disruption. Stage 2 (coalescence) - bony consolidation, osteosclerosis and fusion are all seen on plain radiographs. Stage 3 (reconstruction) - osteogenesis, decreased osteosclerosis, progressive fusion. Healing and new bone formation occur, and the deformity becomes permanent. Radiographs are an important part of investigating a patient with possible Charcot arthropathy. All radiographs should be taken in the weight-bearing position. MRI can demonstrate changes in the earlier stages of the condition, and is therefore important in allowing treatment to be instigated earlier. In stages 0 and 1 the treatment is immediate immobilisation and avoidance of weight-bearing. A total contact cast is worn until the redness, swelling and heat subside (generally eight to 12 weeks, changed every one to two weeks to minimise skin damage). After this the patient should use a removable brace for a total of four to six months. Bisphosphonates can be used, but evidence of clinical benefit is lacking. Surgery is reserved for severe deformities that are susceptible to ulceration, and where braces and orthotic devices are difficult to use. Whilst analgesia is appropriate definitive management is required urgently to maintain function of this gentleman's foot. There is no evidence for cellulitis, therefore antibiotics are not indicated. The cause of the peripheral neuropathy is most likely to be diabetes here, rather than B12 deficiency (when vitamin B would be indicated). Reference: Botek G, et al. Charcot neuroarthropathy: An often overlooked complication of diabetes. Cleve Clin J Med. 2010;77:593-9.

questions.question: A 25-year-old lady presents with multiple ill-defined, polycyclic erythematous rash on face, neck, and trunk. Some of the rash is papular with scaling. Some of these have healed without any scarring. These are exacerbated by exposure to sunlight. There is no other significant history. Her blood tests are as follows: Hb 111 g/L (115-165) WBC 8.9 ×10 /L (4-11) Neutrophils 89% (40-75) Platelet 166 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 16 mm/hr (0-20) CRP 3 mg/L (<10) Urea, electrolytes and creatinine are normal. Anti-nuclear antibody positive 1:320 Anti-dsDNA antibody negative Anti-Ro antibody positive Anti-La antibody negative What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This patient has classic subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SACLE). SACLE is ANA positive in 60% patients. However, only 10-15% progress to SLE with moderate disease activity. Eighty per cent of patients are anti-Ro antibody positive. Skin disease may occur as part of SLE, or be present as cutaneous lupus erythematosus (frequently without any systemic disease), and with variable chance of progression to SLE. Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SACLE) Acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (ACLE) are examples of cutaneous lupus erythematosus which may or may not progress to SLE. However, acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus often accompanies flare of systemic disease. ACLE presents as diffuse erythema, maculopapular rash, photosensitivity, and oral ulcers, while DLE presents as well defined scaly plaques, which heal with central scarring.

questions.question: A 68-year-old male smoker presents with progressive difficulty in climbing stairs. He also has difficulty in picking things off the shelf. He has 4/5 power proximally, with intact reflexes and downward going plantars. Polymyositis was diagnosed based on the following blood tests, and muscle biopsy: Hb 121 g/L (130-180) WBC 7.8 ×10 /L (4-11) Neutrophils 84% (40-75) Platelet 180 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 66 mm/hr (0-20) CK 220 IU/L (24-195) CRP 135 mg/L (<10) Urea, electrolytes and creatinine are normal. CXR is also normal. Anti-nuclear antibody negative 1:6400 Anti-ENA antibody negative Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: Myositis associates with malignancy. The association between myositis and malignancy is stronger for dermatomyositis, than for polymyositis. Patients with polymyositis without any associated antibodies (for example, anti-Jo1, anti-Pm/Scl) should be screened for malignancies which are known to associate with myositis, namely ovary, stomach, pancreas, colon, lung, and breast in women. However, this is not an exhaustive list

questions.question: A 58-year-old man presents with a few weeks history of progressive difficulty in getting up and down stairs, and in getting up from chairs. He also notices that picking things off the shelf are difficult for him. On examination, the power is 4/5 proximally, with intact reflexes and downward going plantars. Recent blood tests are as follows: Hb 121 g/L (130-180) WBC 7.8 ×10 /L (4-11) Neutrophils 84% (40-75) Platelet 180 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 66 mm/hr (0-20) CK 350 IU/L (24-195) CRP 135 mg/L (<10) Urea, electrolytes and creatinine are normal. Anti-nuclear antibody positive 1:6400 Anti-ENA antibody negative What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This man has polymyositis. He does not have any rash. Dermatomyositis associates with Gottron's papules on hands, and a periorbital heliotrope rash. Inclusion body myositis occurs in older people, has an insidious onset, and does not associate with striking elevations in CK. Objective weakness does not occur in polymyalgia rheumatica.

questions.question: This 55-year-old man presented with a painful, swollen finger and a fever (37.7°C). What is likely to be found on microscopy of aspirated synovial fluid?
options: A. Bipyramidal crystals that exhibit strong positive birefringence under polarised light
B. Gram positive cocci in clusters
C. Rhomboid crystals that exhibit weak positive birefringence under polarised light
D. Small, non-birefringent crystals visible only under electron microscopy
E. Needle-shaped crystals that exhibit strong negative birefringence under polarised light
questions.explanation: An acute attack of monoarticular arthritis is typical of gout. Agonising pain is usually accompanied by joint swelling, redness and tenderness, often with a low-grade fever. Urate crystals are needle-shaped, and exhibit strong negative birefringence under polarised light microscopy. The crystals described in the other answer options include: Calcium oxalate crystals - Bipyramidal crystals that exhibit strong positive birefringence under polarised light Calcium pyrophosphate crystals - Rhomboid crystals that exhibit weak positive birefringence under polarised light Calcium hydroxyapatite crystals - Small, non-birefringent crystals visible only under electron microscopy. Septic arthritis caused by Staphylococcus aureus (described in the second answer option) is a possibility but would typically be associated with a higher temperature and other systemic symptoms. The diagnosis can only be definitively excluded by joint aspiration, but the most likely diagnosis remains gout in this scenario.

questions.question: You are asked to see a 36-year-old man with a four year history of recurrent episodes of asymmetrical joint pains involving his knees, ankles and elbows. Two to four joints tend to be affected at any one time and each joint may be affected from two to four weeks each time. In the last decade he has also had recurrent painful mouth sores. On this occasion, he also complains of a severe occipital headache, mild abdominal pain and some discomfort on passing urine. On examination, his temperature is 38°C. His left knee and right ankle joints are painful, swollen and tender. Superficial thrombophlebitis is noted in the right leg. Investigations show: Hb 99 g/L (130-180) WCC 11.6 ×10 /L (4-11) Platelets 420 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 60 mm/hr (0-15) Plasma sodium 138 mmol/L (137-144) Plasma potassium 4.3 mmol/L (3.5-4.9) Plasma urea 6.9 mmol/L (2.5-7.5) Plasma creatinine 95 µmol/L (60-110) Plasma glucose 5.8 mmol/L (3.0-6.0) What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Behçet's syndrome is characterised by: Recurrent oral and genital ulcers Uveitis Seronegative arthritis Central nervous system symptoms Fever Thrombophlebitis Erythema nodosum Abdominal symptoms, and Vasculitis. The clinical course is often one of exacerbations and remissions.

questions.question: A 35-year-old lady presented with Raynaud's phenomenon, and skin tightness. She had sclerodactyly, skin thickening to the shoulders, and bi-basal crepitations. A HRCT chest showed ground glass changes, and she was commenced on monthly IV cyclophosphamide (1 gm/month) for six months, and oral prednisolone (10 mg/day). Over a period of few weeks she became unwell, developed exertional shortness of breath, and pedal oedema. She had raised JVP, pedal oedema, hypertension, and bi-basal crepitations. Recent tests are as follows: 0 Week 1 Weeks 3 Weeks Hb (g/L) 125 120 109 MCV (fL) 90 92 104 WCC (×10 /L) 9.5 9.4 9.9 Platelets (×10 /L) 180 160 140 BP (mmHg) 120/80 150/100 160/110 Na (mmol/L) 142 141 142 K (mmol/L) 4.5 5.0 5.1 Urea (μmol/L) 10.2 12.6 18.2 Creat (μmol/L) 110 170 290 Urine dipstick Normal Protein ++ Protein ++ Blood ++ What is the most likely cause of worsening renal function?
questions.explanation: This patient has diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis with pulmonary fibrosis. Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis may lead to scleroderma renal crisis (SRC) in up to 10% cases. SRC may present with rapid onset renal failure, malignant hypertension, micro-angiopathic haemolytic anaemia with schistocytes. Patients may develop symptoms of fluid overload. Other risk factors for SRC include corticosteroid use (prednisolone more than 15 mg/day), recent onset scleroderma (less than three years), and involvement of other systems. The underlying pathology of SRC is vasospasm, and treatment involves starting ACE inhibitors. Scleroderma by itself does not associate with interstitial nephritis, glomerulonephritis, and acute tubular necrosis.

questions.question: A 17-year-old Arabic male presents with high temperature, abdominal pain, and fixed erythematous rash on his ankle. On examination, the abdomen is tender. Examination of other systems is normal. On enquiry, he admits to several similar episodes in the past, which have resolved spontaneously after three to seven days. Blood tests show leukocytosis, neutrophilia, high ESR, CRP, and a normal UE&C, amylase, and LFTs. There is a mild polyclonal increase in serum immunoglobulin. A chest x ray is normal and the CT abdomen reveals scanty amount of free fluid. Recent blood tests are: Hb 111 g/L (130-180) WBC 18.8 ×10 /L (4-11) Neutrophils 90% (40-75) Lymphocytes 10% (20-45) Eosinophils 30% (1-6) Platelet 270 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 86 mm/hr (0-15) CRP 143 mg/L (<10) What is the diagnosis?
options: A. TNF receptor activating periodic syndrome
questions.explanation: This patient has familial Mediterranean fever. It manifests as episodes of: fever abdominal pain pleurisy synovitis (large joint mono-articular or symmetric bi-articular), or rash. The rash is tender, erythematous with plaque on the dorsum of foot, leg or ankle. Colchicine is the drug of choice for this condition. Periodic fevers can occur in hyper IgD syndrome, however, abdominal pain is rare, and lymphadenopathy is common. Also, patients have elevated IgD levels (frequently >10 gm/L). The rash in adult onset Still's disease is transient, salmon pink and occurs with fever. Patients also report a sore throat. Behçet's disease does not lead to periodic fevers. TNF receptor activating periodic fevers frequently have their onset in childhood. These are associated with headache and myalgia, and eye involvement (conjunctivitis, uveitis) occurs in 80% cases.

questions.question: A 54-year-old Caucasian nurse with RA was commenced on adalimumab three months ago. Her joint symptoms have improved considerably. However, she has a one month history of dry cough, weight loss, and fever. She has lost 10 kg in last month. Apart from adalimumab, other medications include methotrexate 15 mg/week, and folic acid 5 mg/day. There is no personal or family history of other chronic illnesses. On examination, the temperature is 37.8°C, pulse 100 beats/min, BP 110/80 mm Hg, and SaO 98% on air. There is no synovitis. Examination of respiratory system reveals scattered crepitations, and she has cervical lymphadenopathy. These are results of recent blood tests: Haemoglobin 131 g/L (115-165) WBC 8.2 ×10 /L (4-11) Neutrophils 5.1 ×10 /L (1.5-7) Platelets 280 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 98 mm/hr (0-20) Urea, electrolytes and creatinine are normal. CXR reveals miliary shadows bilaterally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Anti-TNF α agent increases the risk of tuberculosis. This risk is most pronounced in the first three months of treatment. Tuberculosis in these instances is frequently extrapulmonary, with frequent abdominal and meningeal involvement. The risk is higher with monoclonal antibodies like infliximab and adalimumab than with etanercept. In the United Kingdom, patients have a baseline chest x ray and assessment of risk of infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis prior to starting treatment with anti-TNF α. Patients at risk of exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis undergo a Heaf test or a QuantiFERON gold test, depending on local policies, to identify those infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. If these tests suggest the possibility of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, they receive chemoprophylaxis with isoniazid, or isoniazid + rifampicin before starting treatment with anti-TNF α agents.

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman with RA was commenced on methotrexate six weeks ago. Her joint symptoms have improved considerably. However, she has a three day history of dry cough, progressive shortness of breath, and fever. The current medications include methotrexate 15 mg/week, folic acid 5 mg/day, and aspirin 75 mg/day. There is no personal or family history of other chronic illnesses. On examination, the temperature is 37.8°C, pulse 100 beats/min, BP 110/80 mm Hg, and SaO 90% on air. There is synovitis in both wrists, and MCPJs. Examination of respiratory system reveals scattered crepitations. These are the results of a recent blood test: Haemoglobin 131 g/L (130-180) WBC 8.2 ×10 /L (4-11) Neutrophils 5.1 ×10 /L (1.5-7) Platelets 280 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 48 mm/hr (0-30) Urea, electrolytes and creatinine: normal. CXR: patchy airspace shadows bilaterally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This patient has methotrexate pneumonitis until proven otherwise. Methotrexate pneumonitis is an idiosyncratic acute interstitial pneumonitis. It has an incidence of 3.3% in RA. Most patients present in the first few months of starting methotrexate. Methotrexate should be stopped, and the patient should never be rechallenged with this drug. Patients with methotrexate pneumonitis may be treated with prednisolone once underlying infection has been excluded. Methotrexate pneumonitis has rarely been reported to associate with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, and tuberculosis.

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman with SLE affecting skin and joints has been on azathioprine (100 mg/day), and hydroxychloroquine 400 mg/day for the last four years. She presents with a one day history of a large blind spot in the right eye. On examination, there is a positive scotoma in the right visual field. Retinal fundoscopy and rest of nervous system examination is normal. There is no history of headache. These are results of a recent blood test: Haemoglobin 131 g/L (115-165) WBC 8.2 ×10 /L (4-11) Neutrophils 7.1 ×10 /L (1.5-7) Platelets 180 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 28 mm/hr (0-20) CRP 12 mg/L (<10) Urea, electrolytes and creatinine are normal. What is the most likely cause of her visual loss?
options: A. Lenticular deposits due to hydroxychloroquine
C. Corneal deposits due to hydroxychloroquine
E. Corneal deposits due to azathioprine
questions.explanation: Hydroxychloroquine ocular toxicity includes: Keratopathy Ciliary body involvement Lens opacities, and Retinopathy. Retinopathy is the major concern; the others are more common but benign. The incidence of true hydroxychloroquine retinopathy is exceedingly low. Risk factors include: Daily dosage of hydroxychloroquine Cumulative dosage Duration of treatment Coexisting renal or liver disease Patient age, and Concomitant retinal disease. Patients usually complain of difficulty in reading, decreased vision, missing central vision, glare, blurred vision, light flashes, and metamorphopsia. They can also be asymptomatic. Most patients with advanced retinopathy have a bull's eye (also known as target, as in darts) fundoscopic appearance. All patients have field defects including paracentral, pericentral, and central and peripheral field loss. Regular screening may be necessary to detect reversible premaculopathy. Cessation of the drug is the only effective management of the toxicity. Reference: Yam JC, Kwok AK. Ocular toxicity of hydroxychloroquine. Hong Kong Med J. 2006;12:294-304.

questions.question: A 50-year-old Asian lady with severe rheumatoid arthritis has failed on most traditional DMARD treatments. She is currently on methotrexate 20 mg weekly and for the last six months has been receiving regular infusions of the anti-TNF-alpha monoclonal antibody, infliximab. Her joint disease has dramatically improved. She now presents with fevers, pleuritic chest pain and a large left sided pleural effusion, but little evidence of joint synovitis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The most likely answer is TB. All of the other answers are possible and need to be excluded. A rheumatoid effusion is unlikely when peripheral joint disease is so well controlled. Treatment with anti-TNF-alpha increases the risk of opportunistic infections and in particular, there is a significant increase in the risk of TB reactivation in conjunction with infliximab. Therefore patients are often screened for Hepatitis B, C, TB and HIV prior to commencing infliximab.

questions.question: A 33-year-old microbiologist presents with persistent fevers of >39°C, severe joint pains, and swelling of the hands and feet. She complains of a pale pink macular rash, which she thinks may be secondary to the antibiotic her GP prescribed for fever. On examination you find a palpable splenic tip and a single lymph node in the posterior cervical region. Blood tests are as follows: Haemoglobin 113 g/L (100-160) Sodium 136 mmol/L (133-146) ESR 110 mm/hr (0-9) White Cell Count 11.3 ×10 /L (3.5-10.9) Potassium 4.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.3) CRP 322 mg/L (<5) Neutrophils 9.0 ×10 /L (1.9-9.0) Creatinine 83 µmol/L (44-80) Platelets 495 ×10 /L (150-450) Urea 5.0 mmol/L (2.5-7.8) Ferritin >3000 µg/L (13-300) RF Negative ANA Negative Serum electrophoresis Normal HIV Negative EBV serology Negative Blood film Normal TFTs Normal Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This is an inflammatory disorder characterised by fevers, arthritis, and an evanescent rash, which is essentially a diagnosis of exclusion. The evanescent rash, often called a 'salmon pink' maculopapular rash is quite a distinct feature. Diagnostic criteria include: total of more than five criteria (including two major). Major Criteria: Fever >39°C Arthralgia >2 weeks Still's rash, and Neutrophilic leukocytosis. Minor Criteria: Sore throat Lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly Liver dysfunction, and Negative RF & ANA. The ferritin is noted to be very elevated. This is probably an acute phase response, since hepatocytes responding to inflammatory cytokines can increase ferritin synthesis. The elevations correlate with disease activity and act as a marker for the disease. Treatment is with NSAIDs for anti-inflammatory effect, and with disease modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) as required for long term maintenance.

questions.question: A 70-year-old retired sea captain develops weakness of the shoulders and hips over a four month period. He has also noticed weak finger flexors with normal strength in straightening them. He has had some difficulty swallowing liquids. There is no past medical history, apart from a sexually transmitted disease picked up in the South Pacific some forty years before. This was treated with antibiotics and he is not sure of the diagnosis. He smokes a pipe and drinks one or two tots of rum at the weekend. A creatine kinase level comes back at 120. Which investigation is most likely to give a definite diagnosis?
options: A. 24 hour urine collection for myoglobin
B. Muscle biopsy with electron microscopy
C. CT scan of the chest
questions.explanation: The diagnosis is inclusion body myositis (IBM). This is an inflammatory condition that affects the over 50s. Proximal muscles and finger flexors are predominantly involved, but distal muscle groups may also be involved. The onset of muscle weakness in IBM is generally gradual (over months or years). IBM occurs more frequently in men than women. Creatine kinase (CK) may be normal. Jo 1 titres are often raised in dermatomyositis associated with lung disease. Electromyogram (EMG) shows a similar pattern in polymyositis and IBM - small short duration motor unit arrythmias can complicate polymyositis and dermatomyositis, but not IBM. There is no association of IBM with malignancy. Polymyositis and dermatomyositis show a much better response to steroids than IBM. Biopsy in IBM shows intranuclear or cytoplasmic tubofilaments on electron microscopy.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presented to clinic with a history of shoulder muscle stiffness and weakness. This had been present for approximately two months and was becoming increasingly uncomfortable; it was also limiting her ability to complete her daily chores. There was no history of a fall or other trauma. She denied having a cough, but reported some exertional breathlessness. Six months previously, her exercise capacity had been unlimited; at the time of her consultation, she would become dyspnoeic on walking 200 yards on the flat. She had smoked occasionally as a teenager, but had never been a regular smoker. Otherwise she had been fit and well. There was no history of weight loss, abdominal pain, mouth ulcers, dysphagia or altered bowel habit. There was no history of asthma. She denied having pain or stiffness in other joints and had not noticed any pain in her fingers during cold weather or any change in skin colour. On examination she had evidence of fissuring and cracking on the distal digital pads of several fingers. A proximal muscle weakness of 4/5 was noted in shoulder girdles. Auscultation of the chest revealed fine inspiratory crepitations in the lower and mid zones bilaterally. Her PEFR was reduced to 270L/min. Investigations revealed: Haemoglobin 101 g/L (115-165) MCV 85 fL (80-96) MCH 32 pg (28-32) White cell count 8.7 ×10 /L (4-11) Platelets 399 ×10 /L (150-400) Serum sodium 139 mmol/L (137-144) Serum potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-4.9) Serum urea 5.2 mmol/L (2.5-7.5) Serum creatinine 77 µmol/L (60-110) Serum creatine kinase 1467 IU/L (24-170) A picture of one of her affected fingers is shown below: What is the unifying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This lady has evidence of proximal muscle weakness clinically and a raised creatine kinase in keeping with myositis. She also has clinical evidence of interstitial lung disease with fine inspiratory crepititations on auscultation and a reduced peak flow reading. The picture of her hands shows the typical mechanics hands found in a subtype of polymyositis called antisynthetase syndrome or Jo-1 syndrome. She does not have the typical rash (Gottron's papules, heliotrope rash) of dermatomyositis. She does not have features of systemic sclerosis (sclerodactyly, calcinosis, dysphagia, Raynaud's) and her nail fold capillary microscopy is normal. Polymyalgia rheumatica occurs in patients over the age of 50 and presents with shoulder or hip girdle pain and stiffness as opposed to weakness. She does not have features of systemic lupus erythematosus (Raynaud's, alopecia, mouth ulcers). It must be noted however that interstitial lung disease may occur in SLE and systemic sclerosis.

questions.question: A 30-year-old male company director is referred to you from the Emergency department with a 24 hour history of a painful and swollen left knee. He denies any history of trauma and does not have any previous history of joint problems. Over the last two days, he has also noticed redness and soreness in both eyes. He is married, a non-smoker and consumes about 10 units of alcohol weekly. He has returned from a business trip to Amsterdam a fortnight ago. On examination, his temperature is 38.5°C. His eyes are red and he has a brown macular rash on the soles of his feet. His left knee is hot, swollen and tender to palpate. No other joint appears to be affected. Investigations show: Hb 129 g/L (130-180) WBC 14.0 ×10 /L (4-11) Platelets 200 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 75 mm/hr (0-15) Plasma sodium 140 mmol/L (137-144) Plasma potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-4.9) Plasma urea 5.6 mmol/L (2.5-7.5) Plasma creatinine 100 µmol/L (60-110) Blood cultures No growth after 48 hours Urinalysis No blood, glucose or protein detected Knee x ray Soft tissue swelling around left knee What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Reactive arthritisis classically a clinical triad of urethritis, conjunctivitis and seronegative arthritis, mainly affecting the large weight-bearing joints (usually knee and ankle). However, not all three symptoms are always seen in a patient. It can be triggered by either a dysenteric infection or a sexually transmitted infection. The characteristic rash seen is keratoderma blenorrhagica, a brown macular rash usually seen on the palms and soles. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are the mainstay of therapy. Antibiotics given at the time of the non-gonococcal venereal infection will reduce the likelihood of that person developing reactive arthritis.

questions.question: A 54-year-old man with RA was commenced on methotrexate six months ago. His joint symptoms have improved considerably. He is currently on methotrexate 15 mg/week, folic acid 5 mg/day, and hydroxychloroquine 200 mg bd. Regular monitoring blood tests have been normal till now. These are the results of a recent blood test: Haemoglobin 131 g/L (130-180) WBC 8.2 ×10 /L (4-11) Neutrophils 5.1 ×10 /L (1.5-7) Platelets 280 ×10 /L (150-400) AST 185 IU/mL (1-31 U/L) ALT 220 IU/ml (5-35 U/L) Bilirubin 34 μmol/L (1-22) Alkaline phosphatase 85 U/L (45-105 U/L - over 14 years) Urea, electrolytes and creatinine: normal What is the most likely cause of his deranged liver function tests?
questions.explanation: This patient has hepatitis due to methotrexate. In the first instance the drug should be discontinued and liver function tests (LFTs) should be monitored closely. If the LFTs fail to normalise, ultrasound scan of abdomen and hepatitis autoimmune serology should be arranged. Autoimmune hepatitis can be associated with rheumatoid arthritis, but this is much less common than methotrexate induced hepatotoxicity.

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman is admitted with a week's history of fever, chills, nausea, vomiting and joint pain. Her GP had prescribed her a five day course of amoxicillin with no real improvement. She complained of use-related pain in her distal interphalangeal joints and knees and is known to have osteoarthritis. However, the pain she was experiencing now was far more severe than usual and she had not noted swelling of those joints previously. She denied any cough, sore throat or dysuria. Past medical history included diabetes mellitus, hypertension, coronary artery disease and gout. The gout had been diagnosed by aspiration of fluid from her first metatarsophalangeal joint during her first episode eight years previously. She had experienced several recurrences, all in the great toe, but had not had a gouty attack since allopurinol was prescribed three years ago. Her medications included furosemide, propranolol, captopril, allopurinol and an aspirin. She had no known drug allergies. On examination, she was obese and acutely unwell. No rash was noted. Her temperature was 39.8°C, pulse 96 beats/min, BP 190/100 mmHg. Heart sounds were normal with a soft systolic murmur heard at the apex. Chest examination revealed mild bilateral coarse crepitations. Abdomen was non-tender and bowel sounds were normal. Several hard nodules were present in the distal interphalangeal joints of the hands. The right knee had a large effusion and was warm, erythematous and tender. Investigations showed: Hb 100 g/L (115-165) WCC 22.1 ×10 /L (4-11) Platelets 350 ×10 /L (150-400) Plasma sodium 144 mmol/L (137-144) Plasma potassium3.8 mmol/L (3.5-4.9) Plasma urea 7.1 mmol/L (2.5-7.5) Plasma creatinine 110 µmol/L (60-110) Plasma bilirubin 55 µmol/L (1-22) Plasma aspartate transaminase 27 U/L (1-31) Plasma alkaline phosphatase 120 U/L (45-105) Plasma albumin 40 g/L (37-49) Chest x ray Mild cardiomegaly Blood culturesNo growth after 24 hours Urinalysis No blood, glucose or protein detected. Apart from acute gout, which do you think is the most likely diagnosis from the list below?
questions.explanation: This patient has an acute monoarticular arthritis. Differential diagnoses will include gout, septic arthritis, acute pseudogout and trauma-induced arthritis (although the latter two are not included in the list). Dehydration from vomiting would be a good precipitant for an acute attack of gout, although the knee is less commonly involved in gout than the other joints of the foot. However, the knee is a typical location for pseudogout, along with the wrist. Septic arthritis is the most likely other diagnosis because of the concomitant rigors and since in most cases only a single joint is affected, with the knee being most commonly involved. The negative blood cultures may be due to the recent use of amoxicillin. The patient also has several risk factors for septic arthritis, namely: diabetes mellitus age over 60 years, and underlying articular disease (osteoarthritis). Symptoms of osteoarthritis rarely fluctuate as dramatically as seen in this case. In addition, systemic symptoms are unusual in osteoarthritis. The arthritis of rheumatic fever is classically migratory, involving several joints in sequence. Rheumatoid arthritis typically affects the proximal interphalangeal, metacarpophalangeal and wrists joints. Arthrocentesis of the right knee is the single most important test to perform at this point as it is the best way to distinguish between infection and crystals, the two most likely contenders of acute monoarthritis.

questions.question: A 56-year-old man with acute polyarticular gout was commenced on colchicine (500 mcg b.d). Two weeks after the acute attack subsided he was commenced on allopurinol (300 mg/day), and the colchicine was continued. His other medicines included aspirin, omeprazole, furosemide, and insulin. A few weeks later, he saw his GP with widespread non-blanching purpuric rash, fever, and malaise. The following are the results of his recent blood tests: Haemoglobin 121 g/L (130 - 180) WBC 11.9 ×10 /L (4-11) Neutrophils 6.1 ×10 /L (1.5-7.0) Lymphocytes 2.1 ×10 /L (1.5-4.0) Eosinophils 3.0 ×10 /L (0.04-0.4) Platelets 480 ×10 /L (150-400) AST 185 IU/L (1-31) ALT 220 IU/L (5-35) Bilirubin 34 μmol/L (1-22) Alkaline phosphatase 85 IU/L (45-105) Urea, electrolytes and creatinine: normal What is the next step in his management?
options: C. Start antihistamines, prednisolone and continue current medicines
D. Stop, and restart allopurinol once blood tests normalise
E. Stop, and restart colchicine once blood tests normalise
questions.explanation: 0.1-0.4 % allopurinol treated patients develop allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS). This can present as a severe multi-organ disease, with rash, hepatic and renal dysfunction, eosinophilia, and vasculitis, and has 20-25% mortality. Risk factors for this include renal impairment, thiazide diuretic use, and recent initiation of allopurinol (weeks/months). AHS is caused by the direct toxic effects of oxypurinol, or by T cell activating effects of oxypurinol, allopurinol. Patients with AHS should not be rechallenged with the drug. Two per cent of patients on allopurinol develop itchy maculopapular rashes, and between 5-10% develop gastrointestinal dysfunction, and deranged liver function tests (LFTs). Allopurinol increases the anticoagulant effect of warfarin, and 20% of patients on allopurinol, who are prescribed amoxicillin or ampicillin, develop a rash.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man presents with Raynaud's phenomenon and progressive difficulty in climbing stairs. He has also noticed cracking and peeling of the skin on the fingertips and on the lateral aspect of his hands. On examination, the power is 4/5 proximally, with intact reflexes and downward going plantars. Recent blood tests are as follows: Hb 131 g/L (130-180) WBC 9.9 ×10 /L (4-11) Neutrophils 88% (40-75) Platelet 196 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 66 mm/hr (0-20) CK 1200 IU/mL (24-195) CRP 131 mg/L (<10) Urea, electrolytes and creatinine are normal. Liver function tests normal Anti-nuclear antibody negative Anti-dsDNA antibody negative Anti-Ro/La antibody negative Anti-Jo1 antibody positive What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This man has anti-synthetase syndrome. Anti-synthetase syndrome associates with Raynaud's phenomenon Myositis Fibrosing alveolitis, and Typical mechanic's hands (thickened, cracking, and peeling skin). He does not have dermatomyositis as it associates with Gottron's papules on hands (on metacarpophalangeal joints [MCPJs] and interphalangeal joints [IPJs],), a periorbital (purple) heliotrope rash, and a similar rash on anterior neck (V sign), back (shawl sign), or on thighs (holster sign). On the face the rash does not spare the nasolabial fold. Inclusion body myositis occurs in older people, has an insidious onset, and does not associate with striking elevations in CK. Objective weakness does not occur in polymyalgia rheumatica. He is ANA and dsDNA negative, which makes systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) very unlikely.

questions.question: A 65-year-old lady with RA (RF positive, anti-CCP positive) presented with headache, and blurred vision in the right eye. She is on methotrexate 20 mg/week and folic acid 5 mg/day. Her arthritis is well controlled, with no swollen or tender joints. On examination, the right eye is red, there is a corneal opacity, and there is intense photophobia in the right eye. Her FBC, U&E, and LFTs are normal. CRP is 120 mg/L. A swab of the corneal lesion did not grow any organisms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Patients with RA frequently have eye complications. These include: Episcleritis (red, tender, superficial painful lesions, well localised) Scleritis (blue dusky, tender, painful lesions) Keratitis (photophobia, visual disturbance), and Corneal ulcers. In severe cases there may also be scleromalacia perforans or corneal melts. Felty's syndrome is a triad of splenomegaly, rheumatoid arthritis, and pancytopenia (predominantly neutropenia) in someone with longstanding seropositive RA. Caplan's syndrome is co-existence of pulmonary nodulosis and pneumoconiosis.

questions.question: This 48-year-old Turkish woman presented with a left ilio-femoral deep vein thrombosis. These lesions have appeared on her tongue four times in the past six months. Which of the following HLA associations is found with increased frequency in patients with this disease?
questions.explanation: The slide shows ulcers on the tongue in a patient with a history of recurrent similar episodes, and a history of venous thrombosis. The diagnosis is Behcet's disease which is a rare multisystem vasculitis. Clinical features include the classical triad of: 1. Recurrent oral ulceration 2. Recurrent genital ulceration, and 3. Iritis. Arterial and venous thromboses are well recognised. Patients may exhibit pathergy (development of pustules at venepuncture sites). HLA B5 is associated with ocular disease; HLA B5 is associated with recurrent oral ulcers.

questions.question: A 22-year-old patient with SLE for last six years presents with sudden onset shortness of breath for last two days. On examination, the pulse is 105/min, BP 110/70 mm Hg, SaO of 93% on air. Other organ system examination is normal. FBC, U&E, INR are normal. D-dimers are positive. A chest radiograph and ECG are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.explanation: Patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) are at risk of anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome (APAS). APAS is present if the patient has Anticardiolipin antibodies or lupus anticoagulant on two occasions over a period of 12 weeks and either has had A thrombus, or A history of recurrent less than 10 week pregnancy loss or One pregnancy loss greater than 10 weeks in gestation when other causes of pregnancy loss have been excluded.
