Patients with APAS and another autoimmune condition are said to have secondary APAS, while those with APAS where no associated autoimmune condition can be identified are said to have primary APAS. Other causes of shortness of breath in SLE, like shrinking lung syndrome, and pneumonitis do not present acutely, and therefore pulmonary function test or HRCT are unlikely to be of any benefit.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man presented with a four week history of pleuritic chest pain associated with shortness of breath and dry cough. He also reported weight loss of nearly 10 kg in the past six months. He had a past history of myocardial infarction 20 years earlier from which he had made a good recovery. He did not suffer from any exertional chest pain subsequently. He lived alone and had not seen his general practitioner for two years. He seldom saw his general practitioner, but had attended the surgery twice recently with mild recurrent pain in his left knee that responded well to treatment with simple analgesia. He was an ex-smoker of 15 cigarettes per day, having given up smoking 10 years previously. His only medication was aspirin. On examination of his chest he had reduced expansion, dull percussion note and decreased breath sounds on the right. A chest x ray confirmed a right-sided pleural effusion. Analysis of a pleural aspirate revealed: Pleural fluid protein content 42 g/L Pleural fluid glucose 2.0 mmol/L What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The pleural fluid protein is greater than 35 g/L which demonstrates it is an exudate and effectively excludes cardiac failure. If pleural fluid protein is 25-35 g/L then Light's criteria are more accurate in determining whether the effusion is an exudate or transudate. It is an exudate if one or more of the following criteria are met 1. Pleural fluid protein divided by serum protein greater than 0.5 2. Pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) divided by serum LDH greater than 0.6 3. Pleural fluid LDH greater than 2/3rds upper limits of normal serum LDH. The pleural glucose level is low. Levels less than 3.3 mmol/L are found in Empyema Rheumatoid arthritis Lupus Malignancy Oesophageal rupture and Tuberculosis. The lowest levels are found in rheumatoid effusions and empyema with pleural glucose in rheumatoid effusions rarely being above 1.6 mmol/L. The most likely diagnosis would be malignancy and appropriate cytology and other tests should be ordered. There is no history of RA to suggest this as the underlying cause. There is also no history of exposure to TB, pyrexia or night sweats to point to TB as the likely diagnosis. Cardiac failure is more likely to present with a bilateral pleura effusion and a history of progressive worsening of IHD. Mesothelioma is possible but again no exposure to asbestos has been mentioned.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease presents with a two month history of stiffness of the fingers and a mild photosensitive rash. He had been started on procainamide a year ago. Examination reveals puffy swelling of the hands and wrists, associated with tenderness of the metacarpophalangeal joints. The chest x ray ordered by the GP shows small bilateral pleural effusions. Which of the following tests is characteristic of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation: Drug-induced (in this case procainamide) lupus erythematosus is typically mild, with arthritis, a photosensitive rash, serositis and myalgia. Kidneys and the central nervous system are usually spared, in contrast to systemic lupus erythematosus. Most patients with procainamide-induced lupus produce antibodies to histone proteins.

questions.question: A 22-year-old woman is on sulfasalazine (2 gm/day) for three months for mild inflammatory arthritis. Over the last two weeks she has developed worsening arthralgia, swollen MCP joints, fatigue and low grade fever. There are oral ulcers, and widespread papular erythematous rash. Investigations reveal: Haemoglobin 131 g/L (115-165) WBC 8.9 ×10 /L (4-11) Neutrophils 77% (40-75) Eosinophils <1% (0.04-0.4) Platelet 196 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 66 mm/hr (0-20) CK 112 IU/L (24-195) Alkaline phosphatise 105 IU/L (45-105) ALT 81 IU/L (5-35) AST 92 IU/L (1-31) Bilirubin 12 μmol/L (1-22) Gamma GT 201 IU/L (4-35) CRP 31 mg/L (<10) Antinuclear antibody positive 1:6400 (homogeneous pattern) Anti-dsDNA antibody negative Antihistone antibody positive Anti-Ro/La antibody negative Urea, electrolytes and creatinine are normal. What is the next step in her management?
questions.explanation: This lady has drug induced lupus. Drug induced lupus resolves after stopping treatment with the incriminating drug. The following cause drug induced lupus (DIL): Procainamide Hydralazine Sulfasalazine Carbamazepine Phenytoin Minocycline Isoniazid Interferons, and Anti-TNFα drugs. DIL presents with purpuric, erythematous, papular rash. They do not have a malar or discoid rash. They have antinuclear antibody (homogeneous pattern), are positive for anti-ssDNA antibody, antihistone antibody, and typically are negative for anti-dsDNA antibody. However drug induced lupus due to interferon and due to anti-TNF α agents, may present with malar or discoid rash, and may be anti-dsDNA antibody positive.

questions.question: This x ray was taken of an 80-year-old male who was aware of a longstanding deformity of his leg: However, over the last six months he has been aware of an increasing ache over the lower leg and increasing deformity. On examination he has an obvious bowing deformity of the right tibia with a slightly increased temperature compared with the other limb. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The slide shows the typical x ray appearance of Paget's disease of the tibia. The aetiology of Paget's disease of bone is unknown; it affects the older population and most patients are asymptomatic. The axial skeleton, particularly weight-bearing bones, are most commonly affected. Hyperactivity of osteoblasts and osteoclasts results in bone resorption and new bone formation; however, the remodelled bone is soft. Although the incidence of bone tumors is markedly increased in patients with Paget disease, they only occur in 0.7 to 1 percent of cases, therefore making Paget's disease more likely. On x ray, affected bones are enlarged and have a disordered trabecular pattern.

questions.question: You are referred a 42-year-old nurse who works in a liver transplant unit. She complains of two months of intermittent episodes of joint pains with occasional swelling of the wrists and knees. These episodes last one to three days and are helped by ibuprofen. However, her knee pain is increasingly worse and her fingers are more stiff and sore. About a month ago, she started to notice a rash on her legs which appeared worse when she was up during the day. The rash was not painful and looked like 'blood blisters'. The rash spontaneously subsided after about 10 days, but has reappeared in the last week or so. In addition, she has began to develop painful purple lesions on her ankles. Over the last two weeks, she has begun to experience low grade fevers, muscle aches and recurrent headaches. She assumed these were flu symptoms and has therefore missed several days of work. Her appetite has not been good and she has noticed some weight loss. Two days ago, she began to develop abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. On examination, she looks ill. Pulse 120 beats/min, BP 140/90 mmHg, temperature 39°C. Mucosae are dry with no lesions. Heart sounds are normal with no murmurs. Chest examination is unremarkable. She has mild right upper quadrant tenderness but no guarding. No hepatosplenomegaly is noted and rectal examination is normal. Neurological examination is unremarkable. She has mild swelling and tenderness of both wrists and small bilateral knee effusions. On her legs, discrete palpable purpuric lesions are noted with a few tender haemorrhagic lesions over both ankles. Investigations show: Hb 108 g/L (115-165) WCC 12.2 ×10 /L (4-11) Platelets 350 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 60 mm/hr (0-20) Plasma sodium 144 mmol/L (137-144) Plasma potassium 3.8 mmol/L (3.5-4.9) Plasma urea 7.1 mmol/L (2.5-7.5) Plasma creatinine 110 µmol/L (60-110) Plasma bilirubin 55 µmol/L (1-22) Plasma aspartate transaminase 107 U/L (1-31) Plasma alkaline phosphatase 119 U/L (45-105) Plasma albumin 40 g/L (37-49) Anti-nuclear antibody Negative Rheumatoid titre 1:160 Chest x ray Mild cardiomegaly Blood cultures No growth after 24 hours Urinalysis +++ blood +++ protein 10-20 red blood cells/high power field 5-10 white blood cells/high power field Granular casts detected What test would be most useful in establishing the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A positive anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) result is present in nearly all cases of systemic lupus erythematosus, thus a negative ANA means anti-double stranded antibody is not indicated. Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) should always be done in suspected systemic vasculitis. In polyarteritis nodosa and vasculitis associated with connective tissue disease, anti-cytoplasmic antibodies directed against myeloperoxidase will produce a perinuclear staining pattern. In Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a cytoplasmic pattern is likely, indicating antibodies to proteinase-3. A positive hepatitis B surface antigen is associated with polyarteritis nodosa of medium and small arteries. Polyclonal gammaglobulinaemia on serum protein electrophoresis would be expected in systemic inflammatory disease and does not aid diagnosis. The rest of the tests listed would give non-specific changes and not be helpful in establishing a diagnosis. The patient has necrotising vasculitis of the skin, kidneys, gut and joints. In addition, she has systemic features of fever, malaise and weight loss. The best diagnosis is polyarteritis nodosa associated with hepatitis B. The negative serology makes systemic lupus erythematosus less likely. The negative serial blood cultures makes endocarditis-related arthropathy less likely. Henoch-Schönlein purpura is more common in children. Although, rheumatoid factor is positive, there is no clear involvement of the proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints which is common in rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.question: A 27-year-old man was referred to clinic with a six month history of pain and stiffness of his lower back. He reported that the was particularly bad in the mornings and improved after he had had a warm shower. He worked as a labourer and often lifted heavy objects at work. More recently he had noticed some pain in his left buttock which often kept him awake at night. In addition to the back pain, he complained of increased fatigue that had been more prominent during the previous three months. He denied any weight loss or anorexia. He had no past medical history of note, apart from one year previously he had had an episode of heel pain that resolved after an injection from his GP. Investigations revealed: Haemoglobin 151 g/L (130-180) White cell count 7.7 ×10 /L (4-11) Platelets 250 ×10 /L (150-400) Serum sodium 137 mmol/L (137-144) Serum potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-4.9) Serum urea 6.2 mmol/L (2.5-7.5) Serum creatinine 96 μmol/L (60-110) Serum C reactive protein 24 mg/L (<10) When he had gone to see his general practitioner after the onset of back pain six months previously, the following appearance was seen on a plain x ray of his lumbar spine: Which of the following features in his history should prompt further investigation of his back pain?
options: The findings on his lumbar spine x ray
Nature of his pain and past medical history
Elevated serum C reactive protein result
questions.explanation: This man describes inflammatory back pain. Inflammatory pain is typically worse in the morning and gets better with activity. He also describes pain of a left-sided sacroiliitis and has a had a past history of heel pain which is consistent with a plantar fasciitis. The most likely diagnosis on the basis of this is ankylosing spondylitis. He is also within the age group that commonly presents with with ankylosing spondylitis. His lumbar x ray is unremarkable but this is because it is early on in the disease process. A history of trauma is more likely to result in a disc tear/prolapse and in this case the presentation is with acute severe back pain. His C reactive protein (CRP) result is high, but not unduly so, which is often the case in patients with ankylosing spondylitis.

questions.question: With which of the following diseases is this appearance associated?
questions.explanation: The slide shows angioid streaks, caused by breaks in Bruch's membrane. Angioid streaks may be associated with pseudoxanthoma elasticum, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, sickle cell disease, acromegaly (and other pituitary disorders), and Paget's disease. A useful mnemonic for angioid retinal streak is SLAPPERS: S - Sickle L - Lead poisoming A - Abetalipoproteinaemia/acromegaly P - Pagets/phacomatoses (tuberous, sclerosis, neurofibromatosis, Sturge-Weber) P - Pseudoxanthoma elasticum E - Ehlers-Danlos R - Raised calcium or phosphate S - Short people (dwarfism).

questions.question: An 82-year-old man presents with an isolated intracapsular fracture of his right neck of femur. He is alert and orientated, and states that he felt dizzy and lost consciousness briefly when he stood up. He has a history of ischaemic heart disease and he takes furosemide for ankle oedema. He has a soft mid-systolic murmur that is heard loudest over the second left intercostal space radiating to the carotid area. The second heart sound is muffled. He cannot leave his house unaided due to angina. He requires informal carer support to complete his activities of daily living due to breathlessness. His ECG shows the typical electrical criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy, but no acute changes. He has been booked onto the planned orthopaedic trauma list this afternoon. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Cancel surgery, and perform aortic valve replacement prior to hip fixation
Perform surgery as planned, under general anaesthesia with invasive monitoring
Cancel surgery, manage the fracture conservatively with analgesics and traction
Cancel surgery, and arrange a transthoracic echocardiogram within five days
Perform surgery as planned, under a spinal anaesthetic
questions.explanation: This patient has clinical evidence of critical aortic stenosis (AS) with evidence of heart failure and left ventricular hypertrophy. He has presented with a mechanism suggesting cardiogenic syncope. He is therefore likely to have a relatively fixed cardiac output state and will be at extremely high risk of morbidity and mortality in the perioperative period. A spinal anaesthetic will be a risky procedure due to profound, uncontrolled and irreversible autonomic blockade. A cardiostable general anaesthetic with appropriate invasive monitoring is more titratable and will be a safer option in these circumstances. The patient's outcome is likely to be significantly worse if surgery is delayed. Although delay may be acceptable to amend immediately correctable conditions such as major electrolyte disturbances, arrhythmias and sepsis, it is not acceptable to delay surgery to await echocardiography . Echocardiography will give useful information, but surgery should not be delayed because of it; it is better to proceed assuming critical AS with an anaesthetic technique tailored towards this. If surgery is cancelled altogether, the outcome is likely to be grave, and analgesic techniques are less effective than surgery at relieving pain from proximal femoral fractures. There is no place to await the prolonged recovery from major cardiac surgery to replace the aortic valve prior to fixation of the fracture. Although a transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) will give useful information on LV function, in this case it will result in a significant delay to surgery. There is enough clinical evidence to manage this patient as if they have critical aortic stenosis with LVSD and LVH until proven otherwise. Aortic valve replacement will result in a considerable delay to lifesaving hip fracture fixation surgery. There is evidence of both LVH and LV dysfunction, which suggests that there is already end organ damage that may not be reversible even if the valve is replaced. The mortality with conservative management of proximal femoral fractures approaches 100% in some series. Even as a semipalliative measure, surgery is more effective than other analgesic techniques . Subarachnoid block is likely to result in uncontrolled, irreversible vasodilatation which will drop coronary perfusion and require an increased workload of a heart that probably exists in a relatively fixed cardiac output state, therefore risking a vicious cycle leading to cardiac arrest. Therefore, performing surgery as planned, under general anaesthesia with invasive monitoring is the least risky option as it allows titrated control of vasodilation and a cardiostable technique can be employed to ensure stability. Reference: 1. The Association of Anaesthetists of Great Britain and Ireland. Management of proximal femoral fractures 2011.

questions.question: A 70-year-old male complains of acute pain with swelling in his fore-foot. What is the radiological diagnosis?
options: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition disease (CPPD)
questions.explanation: The diagnosis is acute gout. There are well defined punched-out juxta-articular erosions related to both sides of the first metatarsal bone. This is a classical site for gout.

questions.question: A 70-year-old right-handed woman was referred to the outpatient clinic by her general practitioner. Over the past year she had noticed increasing pain and stiffness in the joints of her hands and was now having difficulty gripping and opening bottle tops with her left hand. On examination, there was swelling over the distal interphalangeal joints as well as the first carpometacarpal joints bilaterally. Wasting of the muscles of the thenar eminences was also noted. An x ray of her hand is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This woman has clinical and radiological features consistent with osteoarthritis (OA), affecting her carpometacarpal (CMC) and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints bilaterally. OA is characterised by Joint pain Crepitus Stiffness after mobility Limitation of motion. The CMC joint is involved in gripping and twisting. The clinical joint symptoms are associated with Decreased joint space Subchondral sclerosis Osteophytes Bony cysts. Joint swelling is bony in nature, unlike the boggy swelling which occurs in inflammatory arthritis. In rheumatoid arthritis, periarticular erosions are typical. Arthritis mutilans is a severe form of psoriatic arthritis where osteolysis of the DIP and PIP joints occur with 'telescoping' of the digits. Calcinosis and resorption of the tufts maybe visible on x rays in patients with scleroderma.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman with Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (glomerulonephritis and pulmonary involvement) is treated with monthly pulsed i.v. cyclophosphamide for six months. As her disease is still active, she is commenced on oral cyclophosphamide (100 mg/day for six months), and subsequently on azathioprine. Of which of the following is she most at risk?
questions.explanation: Cyclophosphamide causes premature ovarian failure and infertility in both men and women. The risk increases with increasing doses of cyclophosphamide and is greater in younger patients. Cyclophosphamide treatment does not lead to breast cancer, hyperthyroidism, ovarian cancer, or venous thromboembolism.

questions.question: A 51-year-old female is referred by her GP over concerns about osteoporosis. She had a hysterectomy and oophorectomy because of uterine fibroids one year ago, after which she developed hot flushes that persist and are troublesome. Her elderly mother recently fractured the neck of her femur and the patient is worried about the possibility that she too will fracture her hip later in life. She is otherwise well, is a non-smoker drinks about five units of alcohol weekly and has a healthy diet. Examination reveals a fit thin female with a BMI of 18 kg/m , her blood pressure is 122/88 mmHg and breast examination is normal. Which of the following would you recommend for her?
questions.explanation: This patient has a risk for osteoporosis being thin and recently having had oophrectomy. Department of Health guidelines would support the use of oestrogen replacement as first-line therapy in such patients. Unopposed oestrogen therapy is most appropriate as the patient has had a hysterectomy and combined hormone replacement therapy (HRT) is unnecessary. Tibolone, raloxifine and bisphosphonates are recommended as second-line agents where HRT may be poorly tolerated or contra-indicated. Although things are continuing to change with regard to publications such as Women's Health Study and Million Women Study, the fact remains that in symptomatic patients, HRT offers the best therapeutic option and in the absence of any cardiovascular risk factors is recommended. The guidelines state that hormone therapy be used at the lowest doses for the shortest duration needed to achieve treatment goals. References: Women's Health Institute: Risks and Benefits of Hormone Therapy

questions.question: This 53-year-old woman presented to hospital with haematemesis. She had been hospitalised six months previously following a similar episode. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The slide shows 'plucked chicken skin' appearance of skin folds in the neck. Elastic fibres in the skin degenerate and calcify, leading to this characteristic appearance. Patients are predisposed to peripheral and coronary arterial disease, and to upper and lower gastrointestinal haemorrhage. Due to loss of elastic tissue, patients with pseudoxanthoma elasticum have an increased incidence of mitral regurgitation, aortic regurgitation and aortic dissection.

questions.question: A 68-year-old lady presents to the Emergency department with increasing breathlessness and coughing up of small amounts of blood over the past one week. She also complains of frequent nosebleeds and headaches over the past two months. She feels generally lethargic and has lost a stone in weight. She is noted to have a purpuric rash over her feet. Chest expansion moderate and on auscultation there are inspiratory crackles at the left lung base. Investigations show: Haemoglobin 100 g/L (115-165) White cell count 19.9 ×10 /L (4-11) Platelets 540 ×10 /L (150-400) Plasma sodium 139 mmol/L (137-144) Plasma potassium 5.3 mmol/L (3.5-4.9) Plasma urea 30.6 mmol/L (2.5-7.5) Plasma creatinine 760 µmol/L (60-110) Plasma glucose 5.8 mmol/L (3.0-6.0) Plasma bicarbonate 8 mmol/L (20-28) Plasma calcium 2.23 mmol/L (2.2-2.6) Plasma phosphate 1.7 mmol/L (0.8-1.4) Plasma albumin 33 g/L (37-49) Bilirubin 8 µmol/L (1-22) Plasma alkaline phosphatase 380 U/L (45-105) Plasma aspartate transaminase 65 U/L (1-31) Arterial blood gases on air: pH 7.2 (7.36-7.44) pCO 4.0 kPa (4.7-6.0) pO2 9.5 kPa (11.3-12.6) ECG Sinus tachycardia Chest x ray Shadow in left lower lobe Urinalysis: Blood +++ Protein++ What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In the case of metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation, the primary defect is a decrease in the bicarbonate level (and pH) occurring in association with a compensatory decrease in pCO . In respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation, the primary defect is an increase in pCO (and a decrease in pH) occurring in association with a compensatory increase in the bicarbonate level. The upper respiratory tract involvement suggested by the nosebleeds makes the diagnosis of Granulomatosis with polyangiitis more likely than microscopic polyarteritis. Goodpasture's disease is less likely because it does not cause a rash. Ninety five per cent of patients with Granulomatosis with polyangiitis specifically develop antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (cytoplasmic pattern) or cANCAs. Proteinase-3 is the major c-ANCA antigen. The perinuclear or p-ANCAs are directed against myeloperoxidase. They are non-specific and detected in a variety of autoimmune disorders.

questions.question: A 65-year-old gentleman presented to the Emergency department with a fever and an excruciatingly painful right big toe which started approximately 8 hours ago. He had been playing football with his grandson during the previous weekend and, because he did not take regular physical exercise, he had attributed the pain and swelling to this. He had tried taking painkillers at home, but they had not provided any relief. On examination, he was febrile (38°C). A picture of his feet is shown below. Investigations showed: Haemoglobin 151 g/L (130-180) White cell count 12.7 ×10 /L (4-11) Platelets 401 ×10 /L (150-400) Serum sodium 137 mmol/L (137-144) Serum potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-4.9) Serum urea 4.2 mmol/L (2.5-7.5) Serum creatinine 96 µmol/L (60-110) C-reactive protein 276 mg/L (<10) Synovial fluid culture negative after 48 hours. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The most likely diagnosis in this scenario is acute gout. Gout is an inflammatory arthritis that typically presents with acute monoarticular pain, due to deposition of monosodium urate monohydrate crystals within joints. Current EULAR guidelines state that the rapid development of severe pain, swelling, and tenderness that reaches its maximum within 6-12 hours, especially with overlying erythema, is highly suggestive of crysal arthropathy. Involvement of the first metatarsophalangeal joint is more specific for gout, and therefore makes this more likely than pseudogout (deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals) in this case. Fifty percent of all attacks and 70% of first attacks affect the first metatarsophalangeal joint. In addition to joint symptoms, fever and malaise are common presenting features of an acute attack of gout. There is a florid synovitis, with swelling and overlying erythema. Palpation is exquisitely painful. Untreated, the attack resolves spontaneously over 5-15 days with itching and desquamation of the overlying skin. The EULAR guidelines conclude that for typical presentations of gout a clinical diagnosis alone is reasonably accurate but not definitive without visualisation of crystals on microscopy. Septic arthritis could also present with the features described above, but a negative synovial fluid culture makes this less likely. It is important, however, to note that you can get a septic arthritis superimposed on a joint affected by gout and this should be excluded as a diagnosis. The photo included within the question does have erythema overlying the majority of the foot. This may lead to candidates choosing cellulitis as the correct answer here. However, the character of the pain is different in cellultis. Whilst it is sore, the description 'excruciatingly painful' should lead you to think of gout. Inflammatory arthritis is a range of conditions which spans rheumatoid arthritis, seronegative arthritis (e.g. ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis) and juvenile arthritis. None of these typically present with an acute, isolated monoarthritis affecting the first metatarsophalangeal joint. A central symptom of this group is early morning stiffness. Reference: Zhang W, Doherty M, Pascual E, et al. EULAR evidence based recommendations for gout. Part I: Diagnosis. Report of a task force of the Standing Committee for International Clinical Studies Including Therapeutics (ESCISIT). Ann Rheum Dis. 2006;65(10):1301-11.

questions.question: A 24-year-old construction worker presents after an accident at work. He has suffered a crush injury when a digger rolled onto his leg. He was trapped for approximately one hour. After review by the orthopaedic team he was cleared of any fractures, but because of concerns regarding compartment syndrome, fasciotomies were performed on the injured leg. His urine output over the last four hours was 35 mL despite a mean arterial pressure of 70 mmHg. His blood results were as follows: Creatine kinase 7503 u litre Potassium 5.6 mmolL Urea 17 mmolL Creatinine 167 mmolL Haemoglobin 140 g/L pH 7.35 What is the most important management plan to initiate?
options: Furosemide to achieve urine output of 3 ml/kg/hour
Mannitol to achieve urine output of 3 ml/kg/hour
questions.explanation: Early fluid resuscitation is the most important measure in the prevention of acute kidney injury secondary to rhabdomyolysis. Large volume depletion occurs due to sequestration of water by injured muscle. Volumes of up to 10 litres in 24 hours may be required. Most studies target urine outputs of 3 ml per kilogram per hour or >300 ml per hour. Furosemide is not appropriate as fluid resuscitation is the only proven benefit in acute kidney injury. Mannitol has theoretical benefits but is incorrect as has not been shown to improve outcome in acute kidney injury. Renal replacement therapy is not correct as not biochemically indicated at this stage. Urinary alkalisation is incorrect as the primary aim should be aggressive fluid resuscitation. Urinary alkalinisation can be used alongside this but has no level 1-3 evidence to support its use. Reference: Bosch X, Poch E, Grau JM. Rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury. N Engl J Med. 2009;361:62-72.

questions.question: A woman on a camping holiday to central Europe, presented with fever, myalgia, and had a history of a centrally clearing rash. A diagnosis of Lyme's disease was made and she was treated with a prolonged course of antibiotics, making an unremarkable recovery. Which of the following ticks is the predominant vector, responsible for the transmission of Lyme disease to this patient?
questions.explanation: Borrelia burgdorferi causes Lyme disease and Ixodes ricinus is predominantly responsible for its transmission in Europe. Ixodes pacificus and Ixodes scapularis are the ticks responsible for transmission of Lyme disease in the USA.

questions.question: An 88-year-old lady was admitted to hospital with confusion. She had a known past history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension. She had been unwell for several days, complaining of feeling hot and 'shivery' with general aches, particularly in her right shoulder. The staff in the residential home where she lived had called the general practitioner who had prescribed a three day course of trimethoprim for a suspected urinary tract infection. On the evening of her admission she became increasingly drowsy during the evening. The residential home staff found that her blood sugar was high and that she had become confused, talking to her dead husband, whom she thought was in the room with her. On examination she was pyrexial with a temperature of 39°C. She was drowsy but rousable, and confused. She was disorientated in time and place but not in person. Pulse was 130 beats per minute and irregular. Blood pressure was 95/50 mmHg. Heart sounds were normal with no added sounds or murmurs. The chest was clear. Her abdomen was soft and non-tender with no palpable masses or organs. The skin overlying the right shoulder was warm to touch and erythematous. She was unable to tolerate any passive movement of the joint. An plain x ray of her shoulder is shown below: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Avascular necrosis of the humeral head
questions.explanation: The x ray shows lucent defects in the head of the humerus with loss of the normally well-corticated surface. This is consistent with osteomyelitis. She has evidence of a joint effusion and the correct diagnosis is septic arthritis complicated by osteomyelitis. Her age and the fact that she is diabetic are risk factors for infection. Milwaukee shoulder is characterised by severe degenerative arthritis of the glenohumeral joint with loss of the rotator cuff, associated with the presence of crystals. Patients often present with large joint effusions. Bilateral joint involvement is common and this condition tends to affect women over the age of 70. Pseudogout can present with an acutely painful joint. Radiological features show patterns of chondrocalcinosis deposition particularly in menisci of the knees and the triangular cartilage fibrocartilage complex of the wrist. The history is not typical of rheumatoid, which usually affects small joints first.

questions.question: A 31-year-old man known to be HIV positive presents to clinic complaining of xerophthalmia, xerostomia, abdominal pain, weakness and exertional dyspnoea. He is noted to have marked bilateral facial swelling and hepatomegaly. Auscultation of his chest reveals a few fine scattered crepitations. Investigations show: Rheumatoid factor Negative Antinuclear antibody Negative Extractable nuclear antigens (ENA) Negative What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Infiltrative lymphocytic syndrome (DILS) can present like Sjogren's syndrome with parotid gland enlargement and sicca symptoms. Extraglandular manifestations are common and it is rare for the patient to have positive autoantibodies unlike Sjogren's syndrome. The weakness is due to a peripheral motor neuropathy. Aseptic meningitis and cranial nerve palsies can also occur. Lymphocytic interstitial pneumonitis is the most serious complication of DILS.

questions.question: A 50-year-old woman presents with dry eyes, a dry mouth, an erythematous rash and polyarthralgia. Investigations show: Anti-nuclear antibody Strongly positive (1:1600) Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies Strongly positive Rheumatoid factor Positive IgG 45 g/L (<15) IgM Normal IgA Normal Kappa/lambda ratio Normal What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Rheumatoid arthritis with secondary Sjögren's syndrome
questions.explanation: The clinical features and the serology are typical of primary Sjögren's syndrome (occurs alone and more likely to have positive anti Ro SSA antibodies than secondary Sjögren's). Hypergammaglobulinaemia is present in 80% of individuals. The normal kappa/lambda ratio confirms the hypergammaglobulinaemia is polyclonal. Autoantibodies include rheumaroid factors, antinuclear antibodies, and multiple organ-specific antibodies (inc. antigastric parietal cells, thyroglobulin thyroid microsomal, mitochondrial, smooth muscle and salivary duct antibodies). Antibodies to Ro (SS-A) and La (SS-B) are also common. ANA and anti-Ro/SSA antibodies are present in approximately 90% of individuals as is a weakly positive rheumatoid factor. Typically secondary Sjögren's has pre-existent rheumatoid or systemic lupus erythematosus before the development of Sjögren's symptoms.

questions.question: This patient is attempting to dorsiflex his right wrist. There is a small area of sensory loss on the dorsum of the right hand, overlying the metacarpophalangeal joints of the right thumb and right first finger. What is the likely cause of this injury?
options: Fracture involving the midshaft of the humerus
Fracture involving the lateral epicondyle of the humerus
Fracture involving the medial epicondyle of the humerus
questions.explanation: This clinical description and photograph is suggestive of radial nerve palsy giving rise to wrist drop. The typical causes of wrist drop are damage to the radial nerve in the spiral groove of the humerus in a midshaft fracture, and also as a result of acute compression. This is commonly caused by the "Saturday night palsy", when the affected subject falls asleep with their arm over the side of a chair. Ulnar nerve injury is caused by compression at the medial epicondyle. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median nerve palsy.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman presented with a symmetrical polyarthritis of the small joints of her hands and feet. x Rays of her hands were obtained and the second interphalangeal joint of the right hand is shown below. What characteristic radiological feature is shown?
questions.explanation: The radiological changes are consistent with rheumatoid arthritis. Rheumatoid arthritis is an erosive inflammatory disease. The characteristic feature is periarticular erosions. Juxta-articular osteopenia occurs early on in inflammatory joint disease. In gout the bony erosions are typically punched out with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges, sometimes termed rat bite erosions. Osteoarthritis results in: Sclerosis Osteophyte formation, and Decreased joint space. Bone involvement in sarcoidosis can result in: Sclerosis Periosteal reactions Pathological fractures, and A lacelike trabeculae pattern.

questions.question: A 33-year-old teacher presented with a three week history of pain, swelling, and stiffness in his ankles. He had a cough and mild exertional shortness of breath. On examination, his ankles were warm, tender, and swollen. Chest examination was normal. FBC, U&E, and LFTs were normal. Anti-CCP antibodies and rheumatoid factor were negative. CRP was high at 38 mg/L, and a serum ACE was 133 (normal 0-65) units. Chest radiograph showed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and reticulo-nodular shadows in lung fields. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis is suggested by the presence of: ankle arthritis bilateral hilar adenopathy pulmonary fibrosis, and a high serum ACE level. Inflammatory arthritis in sarcoidosis typically targets the ankle joint. Rheumatoid arthritis is unlikely as he is sero-negative for both rheumatoid factor, and anti-CCP antibodies, and there is no involvement of the small joints of hands, and feet. Atypical pneumonia, lymphoma, Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection do not lead to this constellation of symptoms, signs, and laboratory results.

questions.question: A 52-year-old insulin-dependent woman with diabetes presents with increasing lower back pain for the last two days. The pain is intense, and she is unable to sleep at night. On examination, the temperature is 37.8°C, pulse 105/min, and BP 110/70 mmHg. Examination of the heart, lungs, and abdomen is normal. She is tender on the T12 vertebra. Blood tests are as follows: Hb 108 g/L (115-165) WBC 19.9 ×10 /L (4-11) Neutrophils 94% (40-75) Platelet 380 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 90 mm/hr (0-20) CRP 200 mg/L (<10) Urea, electrolytes and creatinine are normal. A chest x ray, thoracic spine x ray, and urine dipstick are normal. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This patient has discitis. Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest cause of bacterial discitis in adults. Unlike discitis, epidural abscess presents with neurological signs in the lower limbs. The absence of urinary symptoms and a normal urinary dipstick test makes pyelonephritis unlikely. Osteoporotic spinal fractures present with acute pain, however in these patients the plain x ray film demonstrates vertebral collapse. Acutely painful spinal metastases are unlikely in the absence of plain film x ray changes.

questions.question: A 40-year-old labourer is referred to you with complaints of pain and swelling in both hands over the last six months. The joints are most stiff in the mornings. He takes diclofenac tablets which relieve the pain. His work involves the use of vibrating tools. Examination reveals that the metacarpophalangeal joints and wrists of both hands are warm, swollen and tender. Investigations show: Hb 98 g/L (130-180) WCC 7.9 ×10 /L (4-11) Platelets 430 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 68 mm/hr (0-15) Plasma sodium 141 mmol/L (137-144) Plasma potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-4.9) Plasma urea 5.9 mmol/L (2.5-7.5) Plasma creatinine 105 mol/L (60-110) Plasma glucose 4.8 mmol/L (3.0-6.0) x Ray of hands Periarticular decalcification What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis typically affects the proximal interphalangeal, metacarpophalangeal and wrists joints. Typical features include symmetrical joint involvement and morning stiffness which improves with exercise. Sometimes larger joints may become involved. It causes pain, swelling and chronic disease causes deformity, such as: Swan neck deformity Boutonniere deformity Z-thumb Ulnar deviation of the fingers Dorsal subluxation of ulnar styloid Gout usually begins as a monoarthritis. Osteoarthritis characteristically affects the distal interphalangeal as well as the proximal interphalangeal and first metacarpophalangeal joints. Psoariatic arthritis tends to affect the distal interphalangeal joints as well. Systemic lupus erythematosus usually causes a mild non-erosive arthritis.

questions.question: A 36-year-old Turkish man presents with superficial thrombophlebitis in his leg veins. On enquiry, there is a history of recurrent episodes of oral and genital ulcers in the last year. Some of these ulcers have left scars. He has a history of anterior uveitis. Recent blood tests show a normocytic normochromic anaemia, normal LFTs, UE&C, and a raised ESR (66 mm/hr). A venous Doppler revealed below knee deep venous thrombosis. On which of the following medicines should he be commenced?
questions.explanation: This patient has Behçet's disease. Behçet's syndrome is a systemic vasculitis with an unknown aetiology, which affects small and large vessels (venous and arterial). More than 60% of patients are HLA-B51, and there is an increased prevalence in the Mediterranean countries. It is commonly associated with mucocutaneous manifestations (oro-genital ulceration, erythema nodosum), ocular disease, gastrointestinal involvement and neurological features. Venous thrombosis is a common complication. Thrombosis of major vessels like the vena cava and suprahepatic veins may occur but is rare. Similarly, inflammation of arterial wall may occur, leading to the formation of aneurysm and/or occlusion. Thrombo-embolism is rare as the thrombi are adherent to the vessel wall. Current EULAR guidelines recommend that corticosteroids in conjunction with immunosuppressants like azathioprine, cyclosporine, and cyclophosphamide may be used in those with venous or arterial involvement. These recommendations are based on the widely held belief that the cause of clot is inflammation of the vessel wall. DVT in Behçet's adhere to the vessel wall and do not result in emboli. Pulmonary embolism is therefore rare despite a high frequency of venous thrombosis. Evidence is lacking for the use of anticoagulation, antifibrinolytics, and antiplatelet agents, and routine use of these is not recommended. Another reason to avoid these agents is the possibility of a coexisting pulmonary arterial aneurysm, which might result in fatal bleeding. Though routine anticoagulation is not advocated, in the case of DVT treatment should be discussed with local experts and commenced as required. Reference: 1. Houman MH, et al. Deep vein thrombosis in Behçet's disease. Clin Exp Rheumatol. 2001;19:S48-50. 2. Kaneko F, et al. Behçet's disease (Adamantiades-Behçet's disease). Clin Dev Immunol. 2011;2011:681956.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man presented to the Emergency department with a history of chest pain and fever. He had felt unwell for several weeks, complaining of malaise and fatigue. One week prior to his presentation he had developed left-sided chest pain at rest. He did not have a history of ischaemic heart disease and denied any preceding exertional chest pain or tightness. There was no associated cough or sputum production. He described the chest pain as being like a needle and said that it was worse on inspiration. He complained of feeling hot and feverish, and also complained of a painful left ear. He was an ex-smoker, having given up ten years previously. He drank 20 units of alcohol per week. He worked as a warehouse supervisor. He lived with his wife and two children. There was no history of contact with any other sick individuals. The family had recently been on holiday to Mexico and had returned three weeks previously. On examination he looked unwell. He was pyrexial, 39°C. Multiple firm, shotty lymph nodes were palpable in both axillae and groins. Pulse was 100 beats per minute and regular. Blood pressure was 125/70 mmHg. Heart sounds were normal. Chest expansion was equal bilaterally; percussion note was resonant; breath sounds were clear. A pleural rub was heard at the left base. The abdomen was soft and non-tender with no palpable masses. The right pinna was noted to be inflamed and is shown below: Investigations revealed: Haemoglobin 121 g/L (130-180) MCV 94 fL (80-96) MCH 30 pg (28-32) White cell count 9 ×10 /L (4-11) Platelets 410 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 101 mm/1st hr (0-30) Serum sodium 141 mmol/L (137-144) Serum potassium 3.8 mmol/L (3.5-4.9) Serum urea 6.2 mmol/L (2.5-7.5) Serum creatinine 95 µmol/L (60-110) Serum C-reactive protein 189 mg/L (<10) Blood cultures ×3 sets Negative - Urinalysis showed no white cells, red cells or casts During the course of the admission he developed life-threatening stridor. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The diagnosis is relapsing polychondritis (RP). The picture of his ear shows auricular chondritis, inflammation of the auricle with sparing of the earlobe. This is a characteristic finding of RP, because only the cartilaginous portion of the ear is affected, separating it from cellulitis/infection. Attacks are recurring and may last from a few days to several weeks. Other manifestations include: Nasal chondritis Ocular inflammation, and Arthritis. The sternoclavicular, costochondral and sternomanubrial joints are commonly involved. Costochondritis can manifest as pleuritic chest pain. Involvement of the tracheal cartilage may result in tracheal stenosis and result in life-threatening stridor. Renal disease is rare in RP and in this case there was no evidence of casts/RBCs in the urinalysis. Cartilage can also be destroyed in Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, resulting in saddle nose deformity and tracheal stenosis. However this is not typically recurring in nature as in RP. Tuberculosis can cause an infectious perichondritis but it is also unlikely to be recurring in nature. Lupus pernio is a red-blue discolouration of the nose that occurs in sarcoidosis. Cutaneous lupus erythematosus affects the skin only with either malar or butterfly rash, subacute or discoid lesions.

questions.question: A 20-year-old woman presents with typical erythema nodosum. She has a low grade fever and bilateral ankle arthritis but no other symptoms and has no medical history. There is no history of travel abroad and she is on no medication. Which of the following would be the most appropriate investigation for this patient to aid diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Erythema nodosum is commonly idiopathic. It can also be related to streptococcal infections, acute sarcoidosis or related to drugs such as the oral contraceptive pill, sulphonamides and penicillins. Rarer causes include inflammatory bowel disease, tuberculosis, Behçet's disease and other connective tissue disorders. In this case, a chest x ray would be the most helpful investigation as this may identify bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy which together with a bilateral ankle arthropathy would strongly support a diagnosis of acute sarcoidosis. Investigation of the bowel is unlikely to help in the absence of any bowel symptoms. Viral titres and ESR are non-specific.

questions.question: An 80-year-old lady was reviewed in the outpatient clinic. She was diagnosed with polymyalgia rheumatica eighteen months previously when she presented with bilateral shoulder stiffness and generalised myalgia; the ESR on presentation had been 60 mm/1st hour (0-30). She was started on prednisolone 15 mg daily along with calcium and vitamin D supplementation and she responded well, with resolution of her symptoms within one week. However, her symptoms have persistently relapsed when the dose of prednisolone has been reduced below her current dose of 12.5 mg of prednisolone daily. How should her disease be managed?
options: Continue the current dose of prednisolone
Continue to taper the prednisolone and treat any symptoms with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Increase the dose of prednisolone and add a bisphosphonate
Continue the current dose of prednisolone and start methotrexate
questions.explanation: Corticosteroids remain the mainstay of treatment for polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR). The starting dose depends on patient's weight and severity of symptoms. The optimum duration of treatment is uncertain and is largely guided by response to therapy. Calcium and vitamin D supplementation should be initiated for all patients with PMR who are starting corticosteroid therapy. Bisphosphonates should be added for long term steroid therapy. The usual starting dose is 15 mg prednisolone per day. Patients should expect relief of symptoms within 24-72 hours. The dose should be increased if symptoms are not well controlled within one week. The effective starting dose should be maintained for two to four weeks after the patient becomes asymptomatic. Generally, the daily dose can be lowered by 1.0-2.5 mg every two to four weeks to find the minimum dose needed to maintain symptom suppression. Once the patient is reduced to 10 mg per day, the daily dose can be tapered by 1 mg every four weeks. Tapering should be guided by clinical response. Normalisation of inflammatory markers (especially erythrocyte sedimentation rate [ESR]) are helpful but should not set the guidelines for decreasing or stopping the treatment. An isolated increase of ESR without symptoms during the course of treatment is not a valid reason to increase corticosteroid dose; however, a temporary delay in dosage reduction may be necessary. Approximately 50-75% of patients can discontinue corticosteroid therapy after two years of treatment. Relapses are more likely to occur during the initial 18 months of therapy and within one year of corticosteroid withdrawal. Patients should be closely monitored for recurrence of symptoms throughout the period of corticosteroid tapering and until 12 months after therapy stops. Methotrexate and azathioprine have been used in patients with corticosteroid intolerance or as corticosteroid-sparing agents. These are generally reserved for patients in whom it has been difficult to reduce the prednisolone after prolonged high dosages (for example, 10 mg or more per day for more than a year). These agents should be added to the prednisolone initially, but with a view to slowly reduce and withdraw prednisolone. As with steroid therapy, azathioprine or methotrexate can be discontinued if there has been sufficient response.

questions.question: A 37-year-old woman presents with dry cough, recurrent episodes of sinusitis, and weight loss for last few weeks. This has failed to respond to several courses of antibiotics. On admission, she has a temperature of 37°C, BP 178/98 mm Hg, and pedal oedema. A urine dipstick shows blood 3+, protein 3+. She has bloody nasal discharge. Recent tests show: Hb 121 g/L (115-165) WBC 12.0 ×10 /L (4-11) Neutrophils 88% (40-75) Platelet 490 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 89 mm/hr (0-20) Na+ 138 mmol/L (137-144) K+ 5.1 mmol/L (3.5-4.9) Urea 11.2 µmol/L (2.5-7.5) Creatinine 119 µmol/L (60-110) CRP 104 mg/L (<10) CXR, ultrasound abdomen and pelvis are normal. ANCA positive (cytoplasmic pattern) Anti-proteinase 3 antibody positive Anti-nuclear antibody negative Which of the following is the next step in her management?
questions.explanation: This patient has got active generalised Granulomatosis with polyangiitis on clinical and serological grounds. A renal biopsy confirms the diagnosis, and guides treatment, and should be performed prior to starting any long term treatment. There is no role for azathioprine or methotrexate in inducing remission for her. The optimum pharmacotherapy for her would include IV methylprednisolone (1 gm/day for three days) and cyclophosphamide. IV methylprednisolone may be commenced prior to renal biopsy if clinically necessary.

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman with SLE (antinuclear antibody positive [1:6400], anti-dsDNA antibody positive) presents with a few months history of feeling generally unwell, tiredness, malar rash, and marked pedal oedema. There is no history of breathlessness. On examination, the BP is 130/90 mm Hg, and there are 4+ protein and 2+ haematuria in her urine. She has normal heart sounds and, reduced breath sounds at both lung bases. Bloods show a creatinine of 147 and she undergoes a renal biopsy which shows widespread deposition of IgG within the glomeruli. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
questions.explanation: The combination of peripheral oedema and marked proteinuria in this patient indicates the presence of nephrotic syndrome. The renal manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) are highly variable, ranging from mild asymptomatic proteinuria and/or haematuria to rapidly progressive uraemia. The various presentations are difficult to classify into clinical syndromes and histological classes. Although lupus nephritis affects a third of patients early in the disease it is frequently unrecognised until nephritic and/or nephrotic syndrome with renal failure occur. Histologically, a number of different types of renal disease are recognised in SLE, with immune-complex mediated glomerular disease being the most common. The up to date International Society of Nephrology/Renal Pathology Society 2003 classification divides these into six different patterns: I - minimal mesangial II - mesangial proliferative III - focal IV - diffuse V - membranous VI - advanced sclerosis. Glomeruli appear normal by light microscopy in minimal mesangial lupus nephritis, but immunofluorescence demonstrates mesangial immune deposits. Mesangial proliferative nephritis presents clinically as microscopic haematuria and/or proteinuria. Hypertension is incommon and nephrotic syndrome and renal impairment are very rarely seen. Biopsy demonstrates segmental areas of increased mesangial matrix and cellularity, with mesangial immune deposits. A few isolated subepithelial or subendothelial deposits may be visible by immunofluorescence. The prognosis is good and specific treatment is only indicated if the disease progresses. Focal disease is more advanced, but still affects less than 50% of glomeruli. Haematuria and proteinuria is almost always seen, and nephrotic syndrome, hypertension and elevated creatinine may be present. Biopsy demonstrates active or inactive focal, segmental or global endo- or extracapillary glomerulonephritis involving less than 50% of glomeruli, typically with focal subendothelial immune deposits, with or without mesangial alterations. It is further subdivided: A: Active lesions: focal proliferative lupus nephritis A/C: Active and chronic lesions: focal proliferative and sclerosing lupus nephritis C: Chronic inactive lesions with glomerular scars: focal sclerosing lupus nephritis. Prognosis is variable. Diffuse glomerulonephritis is the most common and severe form of lupus nephritis. Haematuria and proteinuria are almost always present, and nephrotic syndrome, hypertension and renal impairment common. Biopsies demonstrate active or inactive diffuse, segmental or global endo- or extracapillary glomerulonephritis involving more than 50% of all glomeruli, typically with diffuse subendothelial immune deposits, with or without mesangial alterations. This class is divided into diffuse segmental (IV-S) when more than 50% of the involved glomeruli have segmental lesions, and diffuse global (IV-G) when more than 50% of involved glomeruli have global lesions. Segmental is defined as a glomerular lesions that involves less than half of the glomerular tuft. IV-S (A): Active lesions, diffuse segmental proliferative lupus nephritis IV-G (A): Active lesions, diffuse global proliferative IV-S (A/C): Active and chronic lesions, diffuse segmental proliferative and sclerosing lupus nephritis IV-S (C): Chronic inactive lesions with scars, diffuse segmental sclerosing lupus nephritis IV-G (C): Chronic inactive lesions with scars: diffuse global sclerosing lupus nephritis. Immunosuppressive therapy is required in these cases to prevent progressive to end-stage renal failure. Patients with membranous lupus nephritis tend to present with nephrotic syndrome. Microscopic haematuria and hypertension may also be seen. Biopsies show global or segmental subepithelial immune deposits or their morphologic sequelae, with or without mesangial alterations. It may occur in combination with class III or IV, in which case both are diagnosed. Progression is variable, and immunosuppression is not always needed. In advanced sclerosis, more than 90% of glomeruli are globally sclerosed without residual activity. With regard to the management of lupus nephritis a biopsy is indicated in those patients with abnormal urinalysis and/or reduced renal function. This can provide a histological classification as well as information regarding activity, chronicity and prognosis. Cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate mofetil and azathioprine reduce mortality in proliferative forms of lupus glomerulonephritis. IgA nephropathy is a form of glomerulonephritis characterised by the deposition of IgA in the glomeruli. It is a very rare lesion in SLE. References: 1. Contreras G, et al. Lupus nephrtis: a clinical review for practicing nephrologists. Clin Nephrol. 2002;57:95-107. 2. Molino C, et al. Clinical approach to lupus nephritis: recent advances. Eur J Intern Med. 2009;20:447-53. 3. Weening JJ, et al. The classification of glomerulonephritis in systemic lupus erythematosus revisited. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2004;15:241-50.

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman with SLE is diagnosed with class IV SLE nephritis. The renal physician plans to start her on i.v. methylprednisolone (1 gm/day for three days) followed by oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day, and fortnightly i.v. cyclophosphamide. Which of the following drugs does not need to be co-prescribed with these two agents?
questions.explanation: This patient is at risk of P. jirovecii pneumonia. She requires co-trimoxazole for prophylaxis against P. jirovecii pneumonia. She is on steroids and cyclophosphamide both of which increase the risk of P. jirovecii pneumonia. Among other things, corticosteroids cause peptic ulcer, and osteoporosis. Therefore she requires omeprazole for gastro-protection from corticosteroids, and she requires both a bisphosphonate, and calcium + vitamin D for prophylaxis against osteoporosis as she is ≥65-years-old.

questions.question: A 68-year-old lady presents to the Emergency department with increasing breathlessness and coughing up of small amounts of blood over the past one week. She also complains of frequent nosebleeds and headaches over the past two months. She feels generally lethargic and has lost a stone in weight. On examination, she has no cyanosis, finger clubbing, pallor or a skin rash. Pulse is 100 beats/min and BP 135/95 mmHg. Respiratory rate is 28 breaths/min, chest expansion moderate and on auscultation there are inspiratory crackles at the left lung base. Investigations show: Hb 100 g/L (115-165) WCC 19.9 ×10 /L (4-11) Platelets 540 ×10 /L (150-400) Plasma sodium 139 mmol/L (137-144) Plasma potassium 5.3 mmol/L (3.5-4.9) Plasma urea 30.6 mmol/L (2.5-7.5) Plasma creatinine 760 µmol/L (60-110) Plasma glucose 5.8 mmol/L (3.0-6.0) Plasma bicarbonate 8 mmol/L (20-28) Plasma calcium 2.23 mmol/L (2.2-2.6) Plasma phosphate 1.7 mmol/L (0.8-1.4) Plasma albumin 33 g/L (37-49) Bilirubin 8 µmol/L (1-22) Plasma alkaline phosphatase 380 U/L (45-105) Plasma aspartate transaminase 65 U/L (5-35) Arterial blood gases on air reveal: pH 7.2 (7.36-7.44) pCO 4.0 kPa (4.7-6.0) pO 9.5 kPa (11.3-12.6) ECG Sinus tachycardia Chest x ray Shadow in left lower lobe Urinalysis: Blood +++ Protein ++ Which of the following would you expect to be positive in this patient?
questions.explanation: In the case of metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation, the primary defect is a decrease in the bicarbonate level (and pH) occurring in association with a compensatory decrease in pCO . In respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation, the primary defect is an increase in pCO (and a decrease in pH) occurring in association with a compensatory increase in the bicarbonate level. The upper respiratory tract involvement suggested by the nosebleeds makes the diagnosis of granulomatosis with polyangiitis more likely than microscopic polyarteritis. Ninety five percent of patients with Granulomatosis with polyangiitis specifically develop anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (cytoplasmic pattern) or cANCAs. Proteinase-3 is the major c-ANCA antigen. The perinuclear or p-ANCAs are directed against myeloperoxidase. They are non-specific and detected in a variety of autoimmune disorders.

questions.question: A 46-year-old man has for three days had a painful, swollen right knee and difficulty in walking. On examination, his temperature is 36.8°C. The right knee is red, swollen, warm and tender and has restricted movement. The knee aspirate shows no organisms on Gram stain, plenty of leucocytes, and weakly positively birefringent crystals on polarised light microscopy. A knee radiograph shown linear meniscal calcification. The results of recent blood test are: Hb 123 g/L (130-180) WBC 14.3 ×10 /L (4-11) Neutrophils 88% (40-75) Platelet 340 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 79 mm/hr (0-15) Corrected calcium 2.80 mmol/L (2.20-2.60) Phosphate 0.78 mmol/L (0.8-1.4) Alkaline phosphatase 90 U/L (45-105) Urea, electrolytes and creatinine are normal. What is the aetiology of acute monoarthritis in this man?
questions.explanation: This patient has acute calcium pyrophosphate (CPP crystal arthritis - formerly 'pseudogout'), and also has chondrocalcinosis. Calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) is common in the elderly, and associates with osteoarthritis (OA). If CPPD occurs in those younger than 50 years in age, the presence of the following should be specifically sought: familial disease hyperparathyroidism haemochromatosis hypomagnesaemia, and hypophosphatasia. This patient has high calcium suggesting the presence of hyperparathyroidism. Patients with haemochromatosis develop an atypical arthropathy with CPPD and premature OA affecting the metacarpophalangeal joints (MCPJs) (with radial hook like osteophytes), wrists, hips, shoulder, ankles, and knees.

questions.question: A 25-year-old Caucasian farmer presents to the outpatient department complaining of a two month history of lower back pain which is worst first thing in the morning. He reports intermittent pain and swelling of his right ankle, although he did sustain an injury to this whilst running a year ago. Two weeks ago he was seen in the Emergency department with a painful red eye for which he was treated with eye drops. He is a heavy smoker of 45 cigarettes a day and consumes five pints of beer every weekend. He denies any skin rashes or mucosal ulceration. His mother suffered from rheumatoid arthritis and his father had severe gout. On direct questioning he admits to being diagnosed with chlamydia four months ago. On examination his right ankle was swollen at the site of Achilles' tendon insertion but all the other joints were unremarkable. Flexion of the lumbar spine was reduced. What is the most likely diagnoses in this man?
questions.explanation: The history is most suggestive of a spondyloarthritis. This is a group of related but phenotypically distinct disorders including: Ankylosing spondylitis Reactive arthritis Psoriatic arthritis, and A subgroup of juvenile idiopathic arthritis. HLA-B27 is a predisposing factor for all these disorders and is present in 90% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis and 75% with reactive arthritis. It is present in only 8% of the normal Caucasian population. Ankylosing spondylitis is a very disabling form of spondyloarthritis and its diagnosis should always be considered in these cases. The main symptom is inflammatory spinal and with time ankylosing and spinal immobilitiy develops. The pathology mainly affects the entheses. TNF-antagonists are the major treatment advance although physiotherapy and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents still have a role. Reactive arthritis is the most common type of inflammatory polyarthritis in young men and is an important differential diagnosis in this case.  It most frequently follows genitourinary infection with Chlamydia trachomatis, but may also follow enteric infections with some strains of Salmonella or Shigella. Treatment with doxycycline can sometimes shorten the course of the disease, if associated with Chlamydia infection. In general treatment should be with non-steroidal anti-inflammatories, with intra-articular corticosteroids if large joints are involved. This presentation is not classical for any of the other conditions listed above. Reference: 1. Barth WF, Segal K. Reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome). Am Fam Physician. 1999;60:499-503, 507. 2. Dougados M, Baeten D. Spondyloarthritis. Lancet. 2011;377:2127-37. 3. Kataria RK, Brent LH. Spondyloarthropathies. Am Fam Physician. 2004;69:2853-60. 4. Tam LS, Gu J, Yu D. Pathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis. Nat Rev Rheumatol. 2010;6:399-405.

questions.question: A 23-year-old teacher with ankylosing spondylitis presents with headache. She has a painful right eye, and also reports cloudy vision. On examination, the eye is red, photophobic, pupils are small, and the pupillary reflex is sluggish. Although the visual fields are normal, she reports cloudy vision. Recent FBC, UEC and liver function tests are normal. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Patients with ankylosing spondylitis (AS) are at risk of uveitis. Blepharitis (inflammation of eyelid) and conjunctivitis lead to mild symptoms. Corneal melts (perforating corneal ulceration) is the end stage of keratitis which is seen typically in rheumatoid arthritis. Patients with corneal melts have corneal opacities and ulceration which leads to scotomata. Scleritis presents as dusky blue discoloration of the sclera, with associated pain, and tenderness, but does not lead to photophobia, or sluggish pupillary reflex.

questions.question: A 68-year-old lady presents to the Emergency department with increasing breathlessness and coughing up of small amounts of blood over the past one week. She also complains of frequent nosebleeds and headaches over the past two months. She feels generally lethargic and has lost a stone in weight. On examination, she has no cyanosis, finger clubbing, pallor or a skin rash. Pulse is 100 beats/min and BP 135/95 mmHg. Respiratory rate is 28 breaths/min, chest expansion moderate and on auscultation there are inspiratory crackles at the left lung base. Investigations show: Haemoglobin 100 g/L (115-165) White cell count 19.9 ×10 /L (4-11) Platelets 540 ×10 /L (150-400) Plasma sodium 139 mmol/L (137-144) Plasma potassium 5.3 mmol/L (3.5-4.9) Plasma urea 30.6 mmol/L (2.5-7.5) Plasma creatinine 760 µmol/L (60-110) Plasma glucose 5.8 mmol/L (3.0-6.0) Plasma bicarbonate 8 mmol/L (20-28) Plasma calcium 2.23 mmol/L (2.2-2.6) Plasma phosphate 1.7 mmol/L (0.8-1.4) Plasma albumin 33 g/L (37-49) Bilirubin 8 µmol/L (1-22) Plasma alkaline phosphatase 380 U/L (45-105 >14 years) Plasma aspartate transaminase 65 U/L (1-31) Arterial blood gases on air: pH 7.2 (7.36-7.44) pCO 4.0 kPa (4.7-6.0) pO 9.5 kPa (11.3-12.6) ECG Sinus tachycardia Chest x ray Shadow in left lower lobe Urinalysis: Blood +++ Protein ++ Which is the best descriptive acid-base abnormality of this patient?
options: Metabolic acidosis with partial respiratory compensation
Metabolic alkalosis with partial respiratory compensation
Respiratory acidosis with partial metabolic compensation
questions.explanation: In the case of metabolic acidosis with partial respiratory compensation, the primary defect is a decrease in the bicarbonate level (and pH) occurring in association with a compensatory decrease in pCO . In respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation, the primary defect is an increase in pCO (and a decrease in pH) occurring in association with a compensatory increase in the bicarbonate level. The upper respiratory tract involvement suggested by the nosebleeds makes the diagnosis of Granulomatosis with polyangiitis more likely than microscopic polyarteritis. Ninety five per cent of patients with Granulomatosis with polyangiitis specifically develop antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (cytoplasmic pattern) or cANCAs. Proteinase-3 is the major c-ANCA antigen. The perinuclear or p-ANCAs are directed against myeloperoxidase. They are non-specific and detected in a variety of autoimmune disorders.

questions.question: A 52-year-old female presents with tiredness, weight loss, anxiety and difficulty sleeping. She was receiving a combined cyclical oestrogen/progesterone hormone replacement therapy. Examination revealed a thin patient with a pulse of 110 beats per minute, a fine tremor and proximal myopathy. Her spleen tip was barely felt. Initial investigations showed: Serum free thyroxine 41 pmol/L (9-23) Plasma TSH <0.1 mU/L (0.4-5.0) Serum alkaline phosphatase 202 U/L (45-105) Serum gamma glutamyl transferase 40 U/L (4-35) The general practitioner commenced carbimazole 20 mg twice daily together with propranolol. On review six weeks later she looked euthyroid. Repeat investigations showed: Serum free thyroxine 30 pmol/L Plasma TSH 2.2 mU/L Serum alkaline phosphatase 160 U/L Serum gamma glutamyl transferase 35 U/L The dose of carbimazole was decreased to 20 mg daily. After one year's treatment where the patient felt increasingly tired, the GP decided to refer her to the medical outpatient. Two weeks prior to her appointment she had developed a chest infection for which her GP had prescribed erythromycin. At clinic the following results were noted: Serum free thyroxine 9.5 pmol/L Plasma TSH 10.2 mU/L Serum alkaline phosphatase 102 U/L Serum gamma glutamyl transferase 36 U/L What is the cause of her elevated alkaline phosphatase?
questions.explanation: High bone turnover and osteoporosis may be associated with thyrotoxicosis. Bone turnover involves increased osteoclastic and osteoblastic activity, leading to elevated alkaline phosphatase levels derived from bone. Paget's disease is associated with raised alkaline phosphatase but one should apply Occam's razor and not find two diagnoses when there is one unifying diagnosis. Osteoporosis is not associated with a raised alkaline phosphatase in normal circumstances.

questions.question: A 40-year-old non-smoking woman presents with weakness in right upper limb (power 3/5), and right sided lower facial drooping. These symptoms resolve in an hour, soon after being examined by the admitting doctor. Apart from this, she was in sinus rhythm, had normal heart sounds and peripheral pulses. As a part of her work up she has some blood tests, and other investigations. Results of these investigations are as follows: Hb 128 g/L (115-165) WBC 9.9 ×10 /L (4-11) Neutrophils 74% (40-75) Platelet 80 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 10 mm/hr (0-15) INR 1.1 (<1.4) aPTT 49 seconds (30-40 seconds) aPTT did not normalise after addition of plasma. Blood film shows thrombocytopenia, no schistocytes. Urea, electrolytes and creatinine are normal. CT head and echocardiogram are also normal. What is most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation: This patient has antiphospholipid antibody syndrome which is a non-inflammatory pro-thrombotic state in vivo, in the presence of laboratory tests suggesting an anticoagulant state. The antiphospholipid antibodies (anticardiolipin and lupus anticoagulant) cause coagulation defect in-vitro (raised aPTT which fails to correct after the addition of normal human plasma). However, despite the coagulation defects, and thrombocytopenia, the lupus anticoagulant causes arterial and venous thromboses in vivo. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is a severe systemic illness. The classic pentad is as follows, though is rare to find clinically: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia Thrombocytopenia, often with purpura but not usually severe bleeding Renal function may be normal, but acute renal insufficiency may be present, associated with anuria and may require acute dialysis Neurologic abnormalities, usually fluctuating, are common, but patients may have no neurologic abnormalities Fever is rare; high fever with chills suggests sepsis rather than TTP-HUS. Protein C/S deficiency does not lead to thrombocytopenia. Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura does not lead to prolonged aPTT  or TIAs.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman notices an acute severe sharp pain in the middle of her back when trying to lift a suitcase. On examination, she has some tenderness over the thoracic spine. Investigations showed: Hb 112 g/L (115-165) WCC 5.9 ×10 /L (4-11) Platelets 400 ×10 /L (150-400) ESR 6 mm/hr (0-30) Plasma sodium 138 mmol/L (137-144) Plasma potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-4.9) Plasma urea 5.0 mmol/L (2.5-7.5) Plasma creatinine 85 µmol/L (60-110) Plasma calcium 1.75 mmol/L (2.2-2.6) Plasma phosphate 0.7 mmol/L (0.8-1.4) Plasma alkaline phosphatase 386 U/L (45-105) Plasma aspartate transaminase 20 U/L (5-35) Serum parathyroid hormone 14.5 pmol/L (0.5-5.4) x Ray of spine Compression fracture of T10 vertebral body Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of bone fractures, hypocalcaemia, hypophosphataemia, elevated alkaline phosphatase and parathyroid hormone levels points to a diagnosis of osteomalacia, of which vitamin D deficiency is a major cause in the elderly population. Hypocalcaemia may be present depending on the severity and chronicity of vitamin D deficiency. At least initially the body increases PTH which attempts to maintain a normal serum calcium by enhancing its release from bone. With increasing severity and/or duration of disease calcium levels will fall. Multiple myeloma tends to be associated with an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, hypercalcaemia and renal impairment. In osteoporosis, laboratory abnormalities are not present. Paget's disease does not produce hypocalcaemia or increased parathyroid hormone secretion. The serum calcium level is increased in primary hyperparathyroidism.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with RA, on s.c. adalimumab (40 mg/2week), methotrexate 15 mg/week, folic acid 5 mg/day, and prednisolone 5 mg/day presents to the MAU with a painful swollen right ankle. He is unable to weight bear on the right leg. There are no drug allergies. On examination, his temperature is 38.8℃, BP is 90/60 mm Hg, and pulse is 110/min. The right ankle is warm, tender, and there is a tense joint effusion. You have collected bloods including blood cultures, and have started fluid resuscitation. Which of the following is the most appropriate step in his management?
options: Administer i.v. flucloxacillin, and arrange bone scan
Administer i.v. flucloxacillin, and arrange joint aspiration urgently
Administer i.v. flucloxacillin, and arrange MRI of right ankle
Administer i.v. flucloxacillin, and arrange joint aspiration next day
questions.explanation: Septic arthritis must be excluded in an individual with acute monoarthritis. Septic arthritis may be oligo- or polyarticular in the immunosuppressed, and may present without pyrexia. Joint aspiration, followed by microscopy and culture of the synovial fluid is critical to the diagnosis of septic arthritis, and should be collected prior to giving antibiotics. However, this patient has septic shock, and administration of antibiotics takes precedence over collection of synovial fluid, especially if the latter is likely to delay the administration of antibiotics. MRI will show a wide range of non-specific changes in this scenario, for example, effusion, synovial proliferation, bone marrow oedema, none of which is specific to septic arthritis. A bone scan will show increased uptake at the inflamed joint, and will not allow differentiation between infective and other causes.

questions.question: A 67-year-old Caucasian with Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is treated with monthly i.v. cyclophosphamide and oral prednisolone for six months. His vasculitis is well controlled, and the plan is to commence him on azathioprine. He has normal full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, and liver function tests. What screening test is required before commencing him on azathioprine?
questions.explanation: Blood for thiopurine methyltransferase should be checked prior to starting azathioprine. Azathioprine is converted to 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP) in vivo. 6-MP may be metabolised to inactive 6-methyl mercaptopurine, or may be methylated to active compounds by the enzyme thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT). Among Caucasians, 89% percent have normal or high levels, 11% have low levels, and 0.3% people are deficient in TPMT.  As a result, if azathioprine is given to those deficient in TPMT (undetectable levels), it results in severe side effects, for example, myelosuppression. Patients with normal or high levels of TPMT may be safely commenced on azathioprine, while those with low levels of TPMT may be given low doses of azathioprine under expert supervision.

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman is admitted with a week's history of fever, chills, nausea, vomiting and joint pain. Her GP had prescribed her a five day course of amoxicillin with no real improvement. She complained of use-related pain in her distal interphalangeal joints and knees and is known to have osteoarthritis. However, the pain she was experiencing now was far more severe than usual and she had not noted swelling of those joints previously. She denied any cough, sore throat or dysuria. Past medical history included diabetes mellitus, hypertension, coronary artery disease and gout. The gout had been diagnosed by aspiration of fluid from her first metacarpophalangeal joint during her first episode eight years previously. She had experienced several recurrences, all in the great toe, but had not had a gouty attack since allopurinol was prescribed three years ago. Her medications included furosemide, propranolol, captopril, allopurinol and an aspirin. She had no known drug allergies. On examination, she was obese and acutely unwell. No rash was noted. Her temperature was 39.8°C, pulse 96 beats/min, BP 190/100 mmHg. Heart sounds were normal at the apex. Chest examination revealed mild bilateral coarse crepitations. Abdomen was non-tender and bowel sounds were normal. Several hard nodules were present in the distal interphalangeal joints of the hands. The right knee had a large effusion and was warm, erythematous and tender. Investigations showed: Hb 100 g/dL (115-165) WCC 22.1 ×10 /L (4-11) Platelets 350 ×10 /L (150-400) Plasma sodium 144 mmol/L (137-144) Plasma potassium3.8 mmol/L (3.5-4.9) Plasma urea 7.1 mmol/L (2.5-7.5) Plasma creatinine 110 µmol/L (60-110) Plasma bilirubin 55 µmol/L (1-22) Plasma aspartate transaminase 27 U/L (1-31) Plasma alkaline phosphatase 120 U/L (45-105) Plasma albumin 40 g/L (37-49) Chest x ray Mild cardiomegaly Blood culturesNo growth after 24 hours Urinalysis No blood, glucose or protein detected Which of the following is the most important investigation to be performed next?
questions.explanation: This patient has an acute monoarticular arthritis. Differential diagnoses will include gout, septic arthritis, acute pseudogout and trauma-induced arthritis (although the latter two are not included in the list). Dehydration from vomiting would be a good precipitant for an acute attack of gout, although the knee is less commonly involved in gout than the other joints of the foot. However, the knee is a typical location for pseudogout, along with the wrist. Septic arthritis is the most likely other diagnosis because of the concomitant rigors and since in most cases only a single joint is affected, with the knee being most commonly involved. The negative blood cultures may be due to the recent use of amoxicillin. The patient also has several risk factors for septic arthritis, namely, diabetes mellitus, age over 60 years and underlying articular disease (osteoarthritis). Symptoms of osteoarthritis rarely fluctuate as dramatically as seen in this case. In addition, systemic symptoms are unusual in osteoarthritis. The arthritis of rheumatic fever is classically migratory, involving several joints in sequence. Rheumatoid arthritis typically affects the proximal interphalangeal, metacarpophalangeal and wrists joints. Arthrocentesis of the right knee is the single most important test to perform at this point as it is the best way to distinguish between infection and crystals, the two most likely contenders of acute monoarthritis.

questions.question: A 33-year-old teacher presents with a three week history of dry cough, low grade fever, and erythematous nodular lesions on the cheek, nose, forehead and chin. Systemic examination is normal. A chest x ray showed bilateral hilar adenopathy. The lesions on her face were biopsied and showed multiple non-caseating granulomata. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This patient has got lupus pernio, a skin manifestation that is specific to sarcoidosis. Differential diagnosis of bilateral hilar adenopathy includes: Sarcoidosis Lymphoma Tuberculosis Pneumoconiosis Berylliosis, and Fungal diseases like histoplasmosis. Unlike in sarcoidosis, the granulomata in tuberculosis show caseating necrosis. The differential diagnosis of lupus pernio includes: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis Lymphoma cutis, and Cutaneous lupus. The clinical presentation helps differentiate some lesions, but a biopsy may be required. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis patients usually present with symptoms of sinusitis, otitis, or nasal ulceration. The skin lesions include ulcers, nodules, and granuloma formation. The lesions of lymphoma cutis can occur anywhere on the skin and typically appear as a pink-red to red-purple papule or plaque. There are many cutaneous manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus, but the two most common are discoid lesions and the butterfly rash: Discoid lupus lesions are circular with slightly raised, scaly hyper-pigmented erythematous rims and depigmented atrophic centres The butterfly rash, with its characteristic location over the cheeks and nose, is typically photosensitive and appears as a slightly raised erythematous lesion. Frequently, these patients have accompanying arthralgias that suggest the diagnosis.

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman with knee OA and a history of peptic ulcers, presents with a one week history of worsening left knee pain. The pain is increased by walking, climbing stairs, and is debilitating her. There is no history of knee swelling, or injury. The pain is partially controlled by co-codamol (30/500 mg) two tablets up to four times a day, NSAID gel, and fentanyl patches. On examination, she is overweight. There is crepitus in her right knee and no knee effusion. What is the next step in her management?
questions.explanation: This patient is having a flare of osteoarthritis (OA) related knee pain. There is no role for acupuncture or oral corticosteroids in controlling such pain. Such flares are common, and may be controlled by opiates, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)/Coxibs or intra-articular corticosteroid injections. Of these, intra-articular long acting corticosteroid injections are most effective. The need for intra-articular long acting corticosteroid injections should be guided by symptoms, and not by the presence or absence of joint effusion.
